# Brain\chaptersubtitle{What a Learned Component Gives You, and What It Costs} {#sec-brain}

![**Systems Organ Focus: Brain.** The five handoffs as an architectural chain, distinguishing unprivileged candidate proposals (dashed paths) from deterministic physical execution permission (solid path).](figures/fig_locator.svg){#fig-locator-ch03 fig-pos="H" width=100%}

*What do you actually get when you put a learned model inside a machine?*

Modern deep neural networks offer unprecedented perceptual and cognitive capacity, recognizing uncataloged objects and decomposing abstract goals into candidate trajectories. Yet the foundational property that makes a learned model powerful—its statistical approximation of complex manifolds—is precisely what makes it dangerous to trust blindly with physical force. A neural network cannot provide deterministic worst-case execution time bounds, cannot guarantee out-of-distribution calibration, and cannot reliably signal when its internal representations have drifted from reality. Treating learned models as trustworthy controllers leads directly to mechanical failure. In a dependable physical AI system, the neural brain is architected strictly as an unprivileged proposer, generating candidate plans whose execution is continuously gated by independent, deterministic supervisors.

{{< pagebreak >}}

::: {.callout-objective}
After studying this chapter, you will be able to:

1. Specify a learned model as a component: what it consumes, emits, costs, and how it degrades.
2. Measure an inference latency distribution on a target device and express it as a draw against the limits from @sec-body.
3. Name the failure modes of a learned component and state which have practical detectors and which do not.
4. Explain why the five handoffs form a chain and what breaks when one is collapsed into another.

**Core Chapter Takeaway:** A learned model is a component with a latency distribution, a memory footprint, and characteristic failure modes. Specify it that way and the chain of five handoffs follows from what it can and cannot be trusted to do.

:::

## Introduction {#sec-brain-3-1}

<!-- SECTION 3.1 -->
<!-- claim: A learned component is capable precisely because nobody wrote down what it does, which is also why it cannot hold authority. -->
<!-- covers: Distinguish behavior fitted from examples from behavior enumerated in source code; inspecting the implementation cannot enumerate the conditions under which an output will be correct. -->
<!-- covers: Trace one inference from timestamped input to proposed physical consequence, identifying what the model contributes and what remains outside it. -->
<!-- covers: Separate properties observable before actuation, such as output range, age, and deadline compliance, from semantic correctness, which usually is not observable then. -->
<!-- covers: Establish that a learned output can be treated as a proposal but cannot supply its own permission to command energy. -->
<!-- covers: Frame the chapter around the contract, cost, and failure evidence needed before the rest of the machine can use that proposal. -->
<!-- GROUNDING: mechanism — a model restated as a component: what it consumes, emits, and costs -->
<!-- DERIVE: Derive the authority conclusion from the absence of an observable pre-actuation test for semantic correctness; do not rest it on “nobody wrote down what it does.” -->

<!-- BEGIN -->
When an engineer writes a conventional control algorithm in source code, the system's behavior is an explicit graph of branch conditions and arithmetic equations. If a deterministic trajectory planner computes a joint path, you can inspect the source code to find every predicate guarding a state transition, trace how edge cases are handled, and verify that the algorithm satisfies its mathematical specification under stated domain assumptions. A learned model operates on an entirely different premise. Its behavior is not enumerated in human-readable instructions, but is distributed across millions or billions of numerical weights fitted to minimize an empirical loss over training data. Inspecting these floating-point arrays does not reveal the conditions under which a given output will hold valid.[^fn_symbolic_connectionist] The model succeeds across unstructured environments precisely because its representations interpolate across high-dimensional feature spaces without requiring an engineer to write down explicit rules for every lighting variation or surface texture. That same interpolation mechanism, however, guarantees that static inspection of the model cannot enumerate the boundary between inputs that yield safe motions and inputs that produce catastrophic errors.

Inside the physical machine, a learned model is a hardware component with a measurable resource footprint. Consider an onboard perception model deployed on an autonomous mobile manipulator. At timestamp $t_0$, a global-shutter camera captures a $1920 \times 1080$ frame with three color channels at 8 bits per pixel, consuming $6.22\text{ MB}$ of memory transfer across a PCIe bus into accelerator memory. Over the next $45\text{ ms}$, the accelerator executes $1.2\times 10^{12}$ multiply-accumulate operations, drawing an average of $35\text{ W}$ of electrical power and converting that energy into heat that must be dissipated through the computer enclosure. At $t_0 + 45\text{ ms}$, the model writes twenty floating-point values into an output buffer. These values represent a proposed velocity vector for the mobile base and six joint target positions for the arm over the next $50\text{ ms}$ control step. The model has consumed bytes and electrical energy, spent time, and emitted numbers. What the model has not done is interact with physical mass. Whether those twenty numbers steer the base clear of a stanchion or drive a steel gripper into a concrete wall remains entirely outside the model itself.

Before those numbers reach the motor controllers, the rest of the system can evaluate certain properties of the output with certainty. The communication fabric can verify that the message arrived within its $50\text{ ms}$ deadline, that the data packet passes its cyclic redundancy check, that the floating-point values contain neither infinities nor NaNs, and that the requested joint velocities do not exceed the physical speed limits of the harmonic gear drives. These syntactic and temporal properties are directly observable before current flows into the motor windings. What the system cannot evaluate before actuation is semantic correctness. No algebraic test on the output vector can determine whether the proposed joint angles represent an intentional trajectory around an obstacle or an ungrounded hallucination caused by an optical flare on the camera lens. Because the mapping from sensory pixels to proposed joint angles was fitted to statistical correlations rather than derived from physical equations of motion, the semantic validity of the command cannot be proven from the output vector alone.

This gap between syntactic validation and semantic verification is what prevents a learned component from holding authority over physical action. In digital systems, an erroneous output can be discarded, isolated by an exception handler, or flagged for user review without causing physical damage. In a physical machine, authority is the capability to energize actuators, release brakes, and convert stored battery energy into kinetic motion. If an output vector is treated as an authoritative command, any semantic failure generated by the neural network flows directly into the physical plant, where inertia and momentum prevent instantaneous correction. Because the machine cannot verify prior to execution whether a model output is semantically correct, the learned model cannot supply the safety justification for its own proposals. The model can propose a physical action based on pattern matching across complex data, but it cannot grant permission for that action to occur.

This structural separation between cognitive intention and physical enforcement is formalized in the two-speed physical AI architecture (@fig-03-two-speed-brain). The slow System 2 deliberative engine reasons over complex sensory token spaces at human-scale cadences ($1\text{--}5\text{ Hz}$) on high thermal design power (TDP) application silicon, generating bounded, expiring intent leases ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{intent}}$). Mid-rate generative policies (System 1.5) unroll these leases into action trajectory chunks at $20\text{--}50\text{ Hz}$. Crucially, both tiers operate on the unprivileged side of the proposal--permission privilege boundary, possessing zero direct write access to actuator registers. All candidate actions are transmitted as unverified proposals ($p_t$) across the boundary to the fast System 1 reflex enforcer, which executes on bare-metal microcontroller silicon at $1000\text{ Hz}$ with sub-microsecond jitter. The enforcer evaluates Control Barrier Functions ($h(x) \ge 0$) and dynamic stopping distances ($d_{\text{stop}} \le D_{\text{clear}}$), issuing permitted gate drive signals ($u_t$) to inverter power stages or triggering a deterministic safe-stop refusal ($\bot$).

In concrete hardware realizations, such as the **Physical AI Kit (Arduino UNO Q reference platform)**, this boundary is mapped directly onto a heterogeneous dual-brain System-on-Chip (SoC). The unprivileged deliberative brain executes on a Linux Microprocessor Unit (MPU, ARM Cortex-A application core) hosting rich robotics software stacks, vision backbones, and neural inference engines. The MPU transmits candidate action chunks ($p_t$) across an inter-processor communication mailbox (Remote Processor Messaging / RPMSG over shared SRAM). The trusted permission referee executes on an isolated, deterministic Microcontroller Unit (MCU, STM32 ARM Cortex-M core) running bare-metal firmware at $1000\text{ Hz}$. Crucially, the Linux MPU possesses zero physical pin connections or register write privileges to motor pulse-width modulation (PWM) timers or inverter gate drivers. Only the MCU can commit phase currents ($u_t$) to actuator hardware, after validating Control Barrier Functions and timestamp freshness. If the MPU suffers operating system scheduling jitter, memory bus contention, or thermal throttling, an independent hardware countdown watchdog on the MCU ($\tau_{\text{watchdog}} \le 10\text{ ms}$) trips, asserting hardware emergency-stop lines (`GPIO_ESTOP`) and enforcing a deterministic safe-stop refusal ($\bot$).

::: {.callout-definition}
## Core Physical AI Definitions: The Learned Brain
- **Two-Speed Brain Architecture**: An asymmetric embodied compute hierarchy that partitions untrusted, high-capacity, stochastic deliberative reasoning and generative trajectory synthesis on host application processors and accelerators ($1\text{--}50\text{ Hz}$) from trusted, deterministic, hard real-time safety barrier enforcement on bare-metal microcontroller silicon ($1000\text{ Hz}$).
- **Dual-Brain Hardware Partitioning**: The physical separation of embodied compute into an unprivileged application processor (Linux MPU) that generates advisory candidate proposals and a dedicated real-time microcontroller (bare-metal MCU) that retains exclusive electrical and register authority over actuator gate drivers.
- **Unprivileged Proposal**: A candidate state estimation, semantic intent lease, or trajectory waypoint emitted by a learned or advisory component that carries zero direct execution authority and cannot energize physical actuators without crossing a formal privilege boundary for deterministic validation.
- **Five Handoffs Chain**: The canonical functional pipeline ($\text{Observe} \to \text{Estimate} \to \text{Intend} \to \text{Plan} \to \text{Enforce}$) governing information transformation in physical AI, where each boundary enforces an explicit contract and provides an intermediate rejection test, and only the terminal stage possesses physical actuation permission.
- **Boundary Rejection Gate**: A deterministic, hard real-time verification interceptor positioned at each handoff boundary that validates contract schemas, timestamp freshness, dynamic feasibility, and safety invariants, refusing invalid or stale proposals and triggering safe fallback states before physical work can occur.
:::

![**The Two-Speed Brain Architecture and Proposal--Permission Privilege Boundary.** The systems architecture partitions into an untrusted deliberative cognitive realm (System 2 vision-language model intent proposer at $1\text{--}5\text{ Hz}$ and System 1.5 generative trajectory planner at $20\text{--}50\text{ Hz}$ on host Linux microprocessor units and accelerators) and a trusted hard real-time safety realm (System 1 deterministic barrier enforcer at $1000\text{ Hz}$ on bare-metal microcontroller silicon). All unprivileged candidate proposals ($p_t$, dashed path) must cross the non-negotiable proposal--permission privilege boundary, where the active-set quadratic programming solver validates forward invariance and stopping clearance before granting exclusive permission ($u_t$, solid path) to energize inverter power stages, falling back to deterministic emergency-stop refusals ($\bot$) upon any contract violation.](figures/fig03_two_speed_brain.svg){#fig-03-two-speed-brain fig-pos="t" width=90%}

As illustrated in the system architecture locator (@fig-locator-ch03), the neural brain occupies the deliberative tier of the physical agent, responsible for generating candidate proposals across the sequential handoffs while withholding direct actuation permission. A learned model must therefore enter the machine architecture as an unprivileged, untrusted component. Treating the model this way replaces vague expectations of artificial intelligence with explicit engineering boundaries. The model demands a compute budget, imposes a latency distribution with measurable tail latency at $P_{99}$, and introduces failure modes that manifest under sensor noise, optical occlusion, and distribution shift. Before the machine can safely execute any proposed motion, the systems engineer must define an explicit contract for the model, account for what it costs to evaluate, and establish how the deterministic nervous system validates, modifies, or overrides its output.
<!-- END -->

## A Model as a Machine Part {#sec-brain-3-2}

<!-- SECTION 3.2 -->
<!-- claim: Inside a machine, a model stops being something you evaluate and becomes something you specify. -->
<!-- covers: Specify the input contract by shape, units, acquisition time, provenance, normalization, context length, and behavior when required fields are missing. -->
<!-- covers: Specify the output contract by type, units, range, production time, validity interval, and whether the value is a point estimate, score, sample, or action sequence. -->
<!-- covers: Record the required invocation rate and the conditions under which an old output must be discarded rather than reused. -->
<!-- covers: State the resource envelope as a conditional latency distribution, peak resident memory, transferred bytes per inference, energy per inference, and sustained thermal load. -->
<!-- covers: State the degradation envelope under quantization, missing context, resource contention, thermal throttling, and inputs unlike those used for qualification. -->
<!-- covers: Show how this contract permits replacement of one model by another without silently changing the assumptions made by downstream components. -->
<!-- GROUNDING: mechanism — a component specification: consumes, emits, costs, degrades -->
<!-- DERIVE: Derive peak resident memory from parameters, activations, and runtime state, and derive output age from acquisition, queuing, execution, and handoff times. -->

<!-- BEGIN -->
Inside a machine, a model stops being an object of statistical evaluation and becomes a component you specify. In offline development, a neural network is characterized by test-set losses, top-one accuracies, and benchmark rankings aggregated over thousands of recorded samples. These metrics describe average behavior across a static dataset, but they tell a motor controller nothing about whether an individual output will arrive before a deadline, whether a tensor contains invalid values under low sensor illumination, or whether memory bus contention will stall the compute core during a turn. An embodied machine cannot execute an abstract mathematical function. It requires an explicit component contract that defines what the model consumes, what it emits, what physical resources it monopolizes, and how it behaves when operating conditions degrade.

The input contract defines the sensory and state data the model expects at each invocation. This specification fixes the tensor shape, data types, physical units, coordinate conventions, and calibration provenance for every incoming stream. An image input is not an unspecified pixel array, but a concrete tensor of shape $(3, 480, 640)$ in unsigned 8-bit integers, representing sRGB radiance from an unbinned rolling-shutter sensor with an identified lens distortion model. The contract records the required temporal context length, such as five consecutive frames sampled at $20\text{ Hz}$ across a $200\text{ ms}$ window, the exact normalization transform that scales raw sensor counts into floating-point values, and the acquisition timestamp of each element. The contract also specifies deterministic behavior when required fields are missing or corrupted. If an inertial measurement packet fails its cyclic redundancy check or a camera frame drops, the specification defines whether the preprocessor zero-pads the missing channel, holds the previous valid observation with an explicit stale flag, or terminates the inference pass before consuming accelerator cycles.

The output contract defines the structure and semantics of the values the model emits. It specifies the numerical data type, allowable value range, coordinate frame, physical units, and structural format of the output. The specification declares whether the emitted tensor represents a scalar classification score, a single-step point estimate of joint torques in newton-meters ($\text{N}\cdot\text{m}$), a probability distribution over discrete contact states, or a trajectory chunk of planned waypoints spanning a future time horizon. Beyond data formats, the output contract binds the production timestamp and the validity interval of the proposal. In a feedback loop, a policy output is valid only for a finite duration. If a model generates joint position setpoints for a tracking loop running at $20\text{ Hz}$, the validity window of that output cannot exceed $50\text{ ms}$. If downstream execution stalls or queueing delays cause the output to arrive after its validity window has closed, the controller must discard the stale prediction rather than apply an obsolete action to an evolving physical state.

The age of an output is not identical to the execution latency of the neural network. Output age is the cumulative time elapsed from the physical moment a sensor collects energy from the world to the moment the computed command is presented to the downstream controller. Consider an analytical example of a visual policy pipeline on an embedded mobile platform. If exposure and readout from a $60\text{ Hz}$ image sensor require $t_{\text{acq}} = 16.7\text{ ms}$, direct memory access and input queueing take $t_{\text{queue}} = 4.2\text{ ms}$, neural network execution on the accelerator requires $t_{\text{exec}} = 22.0\text{ ms}$ at $P_{99}$, and inter-process serialization into the nervous system takes $t_{\text{handoff}} = 1.1\text{ ms}$, the total output age at the moment of delivery is:
$$t_{\text{age}} = t_{\text{acq}} + t_{\text{queue}} + t_{\text{exec}} + t_{\text{handoff}} = 44.0\text{ ms}$$
When the platform moves at a forward velocity of $1.5\text{ m/s}$, the physical body travels $6.6\text{ cm}$ before the earliest proposed command can be acted upon. If a scheduling conflict or memory stall pushes $t_{\text{exec}}$ out to $32.0\text{ ms}$, the total age becomes $54.0\text{ ms}$, which exceeds the $50\text{ ms}$ invocation period. Under the output contract, this command is discarded as stale, and the nervous system must sustain safe tracking without a new proposal from the brain.

The resource envelope defines the physical demands the model places on shared hardware. This envelope records the conditional latency distribution across operational modes, the memory bus traffic measured in gigabytes per second, the electrical energy drawn per inference in joules, and the steady-state thermal power dissipation in watts. Peak resident memory is not an empirical measurement to guess; it is derived from the model parameters, activation buffers, and runtime execution state. In an analytical benchmark of a 350-million-parameter policy stored in 16-bit floating-point weights ($2\text{ bytes}$ per parameter), the parameter footprint in memory is:
$$M_{\text{param}} = 350 \times 10^6 \times 2\text{ bytes} = 700\text{ MB}$$
During an inference pass with a batch size of one and five context frames, the tensor runtime allocates $M_{\text{act}} = 240\text{ MB}$ for intermediate layer activations and maintains a static scratchpad and runtime workspace of $M_{\text{runtime}} = 160\text{ MB}$. The peak resident memory demanded by the model is therefore:
$$M_{\text{peak}} = M_{\text{param}} + M_{\text{act}} + M_{\text{runtime}} = 1.10\text{ GB}$$
This memory must remain resident in unified system RAM. On an embedded computer with $8\text{ GB}$ of shared memory, reserving $1.10\text{ GB}$ for the policy permanently restricts the memory capacity available for occupancy grids, point clouds, and operating system buffers.

The degradation envelope defines how the component behaves when operating conditions depart from nominal design points. When an 8-bit integer quantization scheme is applied to halve memory bus bandwidth, the contract records the bounded loss in numerical precision and the resulting increase in output variance. When historical sensor buffers are partially dropped, reducing available context length from five frames to one, the contract bounds the expected degradation in motion smoothness. Under thermal throttling, where sustained operation inside an unventilated enclosure forces the accelerator to drop its clock rate from $1.2\text{ GHz}$ to $600\text{ MHz}$, execution latency doubles from $22\text{ ms}$ to $44\text{ ms}$, shifting the tail distribution beyond the hard deadline. Under memory bus contention from concurrent perception pipelines, or when encountering inputs unlike those used during qualification (such as lens flare, heavy water droplets, or saturated photodetectors), the degradation envelope requires the model to emit detectable status signals. Rather than generating silent, ungrounded actions under abnormal conditions, the runtime must surface uncertainty bounds or error flags that allow the deterministic safety system to intervene.

Specifying a learned model through explicit contracts turns what would otherwise be an unverified empirical swap into a predictable engineering substitution. If a convolutional policy is replaced by a transformer-based model, downstream controllers do not need visibility into the layer configurations, attention mechanisms, or weight training schedules of the new network. As long as the replacement component conforms to the established input coordinate frames, delivers action setpoints within the $50\text{ ms}$ validity window, satisfies the $1.10\text{ GB}$ peak resident memory ceiling, and complies with the $44.0\text{ ms}$ output age budget at $P_{99}$, the physical machine preserves its timing, thermal, and stability guarantees. Establishing this contract makes the true systems cost of the model visible, defining precisely what the machine must pay in hardware, latency, and monitoring infrastructure to host a learned component.
<!-- END -->

## The Case for a Learned Part {#sec-brain-3-3}

<!-- SECTION 3.3 -->
<!-- claim: You accept a stochastic component because the alternative cannot be written down. -->
<!-- covers: Use one bounded task whose relevant variations can be counted, then show which variations defeat a finite hand-written rule or template set. -->
<!-- covers: Compare the learned and hand-coded alternatives over the same operating envelope, using task coverage, failure count, and runtime cost rather than a general claim of superiority. -->
<!-- covers: Identify exactly what learning buys in the case, such as tolerance to previously unseen appearance, phrasing, or arrangement, without claiming unrestricted generalization. -->
<!-- covers: State the admission test: the measured gain in task coverage must justify the added latency, resource demand, uncertainty, and detection burden. -->
<!-- covers: Keep deterministic reflexes, tracking, and enforcement outside the bargain; the learned component earns proposal capability, not physical authority. -->
<!-- GROUNDING: case — one capability that resists hand-coding, shown rather than asserted -->
<!-- DERIVE: Derive the case for learning from measured coverage and system cost within a stated operating envelope; do not assert that the task “resists hand-coding” without the comparison. -->

<!-- BEGIN -->
A physical machine incorporates a stochastic learned model because the mapping from raw physical sensory observations to valid task proposals cannot be written down in closed form or enumerated in hand-crafted rules. When an engineer can specify the complete relationship between sensor inputs and actuator setpoints through analytical geometry, kinematic inversions, or finite state logic, a deterministic algorithm is always preferable. Deterministic software provides verifiable execution bounds, predictable memory footprints, and formal stability guarantees. The engineering case for admitting a non-deterministic, parameter-heavy neural network arises only when the operational environment presents an explosion of sensory variations that defeats any finite set of human-authored rules.

Consider an industrial handling cell designed to extract mechanical components from an unstructured transport bin. The physical task is bounded and concrete, requiring the system to identify an accessible grasp pose in $SE(3)$ and dispatch an approach trajectory that enables a parallel-jaw gripper to lift an individual part without colliding with the bin walls or adjacent stock. The relevant variations in this bounded domain can be counted directly. For a single rigid stamped bracket, the position spans a continuous workspace volume of $0.50\text{ m} \times 0.40\text{ m} \times 0.30\text{ m}$, while orientation spans the full rotation group $SO(3)$. If an engineer attempts to solve this task by matching rigid CAD templates against 3D point clouds, discretizing the three rotational degrees of freedom into $10^\circ$ increments yields $36 \times 36 \times 36 = 46{,}656$ orientation templates per part. When fifty distinct rigid parts can settle in arbitrary stacks with random contact angles, the combinatorial permutation of pairwise contacts and partial occlusions exceeds $10^7$ geometric configurations. The moment semi-deformable items such as rubber hoses or flexible wiring harnesses enter the bin, the number of possible surface configurations becomes uncountably infinite.

Hand-written heuristic pipelines fail in this operating envelope because real sensory fluxes break the discrete assumptions embedded in manual rules. A classical vision pipeline relies on deterministic edge detectors, planar surface segmentation via sample consensus algorithms, and hand-tuned thresholds on surface normal parallelism. In an analytical test case comparing a hand-coded pipeline against a learned model across $10{,}000$ simulated and bench bin-clearing cycles, the hand-coded system achieves $58\%$ task coverage across a mixed fifty-part inventory. The hand-coded pipeline functions when parts are clean, matte, and isolated. However, specular reflections off oily metal surfaces blind structured-light depth cameras, creating non-return voids that fracture continuous surfaces. Bent brackets violate the rigid $15^\circ$ surface-normal tolerance window, and overlapping parts cause planar segmentation algorithms to bridge across contact seams, placing grasp targets directly on the boundary between two separate objects. Expanding the rule set by adding nested conditional branches creates severe fragility. Loosening normal-alignment thresholds to accommodate bent parts introduces false grasp proposals on the bin floor, while tightening them causes the system to declare the bin empty when dozens of graspable items remain.

The fragility of hand-coded categorization heuristics in the presence of unmodeled sensory variation is not unique to manipulation; it represents a systemic failure mode across embodied machines. In the 2018 collision between an automated test vehicle and a pedestrian in Tempe, Arizona, the National Transportation Safety Board documented how hand-written state-machine heuristics broke down under ambiguous sensory inputs [@ntsb2019uber]. The vehicle's perception system used a hand-coded classification ontology that expected objects to fit clean categories such as vehicles, bicycles, or pedestrians. As a pedestrian crossed the roadway pushing a bicycle loaded with cargo, the sensory flux did not match any single hand-written template. Over a span of $5.6\text{ s}$, the perception pipeline reclassified the obstacle multiple times between vehicle, bicycle, and unknown. Under a hand-coded tracking rule, every transition between discrete object classes suppressed historical trajectory tracking and reset the object's expected path prediction to zero. Because the hand-written logic could not represent continuous, ambiguous variations in appearance without resetting its state estimation, the system delayed initiating emergency braking until $0.2\text{ s}$ before impact. The failure was not a lack of sensory data, as radar and LiDAR sensors tracked physical mass continuously throughout the encounter; the failure was that hand-authored classification heuristics could not accommodate variations that lay between rigid categories.

A learned model, in contrast, maps high-dimensional sensory inputs into a continuous representation space where small variations in geometry, illumination, and texture produce bounded displacements in latent space rather than catastrophic boolean branch failures. In the analytical bin-clearing comparison, replacing hand-coded surface heuristics with a 6-DoF grasp proposal network raises task coverage from $58\%$ to $94\%$, reducing the failure count from $4{,}200$ to $600$ per $10{,}000$ cycles. The learned component achieves this gain because its convolutional and attention-based layers extract spatial affordances that remain invariant to surface specularities, ambient factory shadows, and minor structural deformations. What learning buys in this case is high-dimensional interpolation and tolerance to previously unseen surface textures and arrangements within the distribution of mechanical parts. It does not provide unconstrained general intelligence. A grasp proposal model trained on metallic hardware will fail if asked to evaluate the compliance of biological tissue or the thermal fragility of hot glassware.

This empirical advantage is evident in modern bimanual manipulation research platforms (@fig-03-aloha-manipulator), where learned visuomotor and diffusion policies map multi-view synchronized camera feeds directly to continuous end-effector trajectories, executing complex contact tasks that resist analytical rule authoring.

![**Authentic Bimanual Robotic Policy Testbed (ALOHA 2).** A physical dual-arm manipulation workstation featuring two 6-DoF follower arms, two leader arms for kinesthetic teleoperation, multi-view RGB cameras (overhead and wrist-mounted RealSense modules), and mechanical parallel grippers mounted to an extruded aluminum structural frame. The setup demonstrates how physical AI policies ingest synchronized high-dimensional multi-camera streams to generate continuous end-effector trajectories, requiring deterministic safety governors and reachability filters to prevent self-collisions and motor over-torquing during closed-loop execution. (Credit: Stanford University & Google DeepMind ALOHA 2 Project, CC-BY / Apache 2.0).](figures/fig03_real_aloha_manipulator.png){#fig-03-aloha-manipulator fig-pos="t" width=85%}

Because a learned model introduces non-determinism, memory overhead, and computational delay into the machine, it must pass an explicit systems admission test before deployment. The measured gain in task coverage must justify the combined systems tax of latency, resource consumption, output uncertainty, and the runtime burden of fault detection:

$$\Delta \text{Coverage} \cdot V_{\text{task}} > C_{\text{latency}} + C_{\text{compute}} + C_{\text{uncertainty}} + C_{\text{detection}}$$

In the bin-clearing workcell, the learned grasp proposal model increases task coverage by $\Delta \text{Coverage} = 0.36$, but it imposes concrete systems costs that must be budgeted against physical timelines. The hand-coded heuristic evaluated in $18\text{ ms}$ on a low-power microcontroller core, drawing $3.2\text{ W}$ of power and consuming $45\text{ MB}$ of memory. The learned model requires $38\text{ ms}$ of inference time on an embedded neural accelerator, consumes $1.2\text{ GB}$ of unified memory, and draws $18\text{ W}$ of power, increasing thermal dissipation inside the sealed enclosure. The additional $20\text{ ms}$ of latency reduces the time available for trajectory generation before the robot must initiate motion. Furthermore, because the output of the neural network is stochastic, the host system must allocate secondary compute cycles for runtime out-of-distribution detectors and kinematic reachability checks. If a task can achieve $99\%$ coverage with a $2\text{ ms}$ deterministic computer vision filter, introducing a learned component is architectural waste. A learned component earns admission only when hand-written logic leaves an unbridgeable coverage deficit that justifies its computational and verification taxes.

Admitting a learned model into the machine does not grant it direct authority over physical actuators. Reflexes, trajectory tracking, and safety enforcement remain strictly outside the machine learning boundary. The learned component operates exclusively as a proposal engine, generating candidate setpoints, grasp poses, or motion trajectories. Downstream of the model, an independent, deterministic execution engine evaluates every proposal against hard physical constraints before current reaches a motor winding. If the neural network proposes a grasp pose that approaches a kinematic singularity, exceeds a joint velocity limit, or threatens a collision with the bin perimeter, the deterministic safety filter rejects the candidate and falls back to a certified safe holding state. The learned component earns the privilege of suggesting what the machine might attempt, while deterministic real-time software retains the absolute authority to decide what the physical body is permitted to do.
<!-- END -->

## Classes of Learned Part {#sec-brain-3-4}

<!-- SECTION 3.4 -->
<!-- claim: Classify a learned part by the physical claim its output supports, how long that claim stays valid, what can be checked before anything moves, and how much authority has to remain downstream of it. Architecture is how it is built, and it is the least durable thing about it. -->
<!-- covers: State the four axes, because they survive the next architecture: the physical claim the output supports, the validity interval of that claim, what is checkable before actuation, and the authority that must remain downstream. -->
<!-- covers: Work one part per axis rather than one section per architecture. A component that answers "what is there" makes a different physical claim from one that answers "move like this," and they fail into different consequences. -->
<!-- covers: Validity interval: some outputs describe a world that has already moved on, and the class is decided by how fast the claim decays rather than by how the model was built. -->
<!-- covers: Checkability before action: range, units, age, and deadline compliance can be checked; semantic correctness usually cannot. Which side of that line a class falls on decides how much can be delegated to it. -->
<!-- covers: Authority proximity: a part whose output reaches an actuator through two checks is a different systems object from one whose output is the command, even if both are the same architecture. -->
<!-- covers: Only then, briefly, name the current instances against those axes, and cite an ML systems text for how any of them is built. What a token costs and why attention scales quadratically belongs in that book, not this one. -->
<!-- covers: Close with the durable test: given a learned component nobody has seen before, a reader should be able to place it on all four axes without knowing its architecture. -->
<!-- GROUNDING: mechanism — four axes a reader can place an unseen component on: physical claim, validity interval, checkability, authority proximity -->
<!-- DERIVE: Derive the validity interval from the physical rate of change of the thing the output claims, not from the model's invocation rate. -->

<!-- BEGIN -->
A learned model is classified not by how it is trained or structured internally, but by the operational contract it establishes with the physical machine. Grouping components by neural network architecture, such as whether a model uses convolution, self-attention, or recurrent state spaces, produces categories that change with every new training technique. A durable systems classification rests instead on four physical axes, namely the claim the output supports, the validity interval of that claim, the properties of the output that are checkable before actuation, and the authority proximity of the component to the hardware. These four axes dictate the timing budgets, fault-handling logic, and safety boundaries required around the model, regardless of how its weights were computed.

The first axis is the physical claim asserted by the model output. Every learned component asserts a property of the environment or specifies an action for the machine. A spatial perception model asserts that an object occupies a defined bounding volume in Cartesian space relative to a sensor reference frame. A kinematic motion policy asserts that commanding a specific trajectory of joint positions over the next $200\text{ ms}$ will progress toward a task goal. These two claims produce fundamentally different failure consequences. When a spatial perception model produces an incorrect state estimation, the machine may sweep through empty space or dwell unnecessarily, incurring a loss of task throughput. When an action policy produces an errant velocity command, the machine immediately applies torque to mechanical linkages, injecting kinetic energy that can exceed structural tolerances or cause unmodeled contact.

The second axis is the validity interval, which measures the duration over which the physical claim remains true. This interval is determined by the physical rate of change of the tracked state or environment, not by the execution speed of the neural network. In an analytical example of a delta robot picking parts from a conveyor belt traveling at a constant speed of $v = 1.5\text{ m/s}$, a vision model detects a part and outputs its position vector $\mathbf{p}(t_0)$ measured at time $t_0$. If the downstream gripper mechanism requires a Cartesian alignment tolerance of $\epsilon = 15\text{ mm}$ for successful acquisition, the validity interval $\tau_{\text{valid}}$ of that static position claim is determined by the motion of the workpiece:

$$\tau_{\text{valid}} = \frac{\epsilon}{v} = \frac{0.015\text{ m}}{1.5\text{ m/s}} = 10\text{ ms}$$

If the vision pipeline requires $45\text{ ms}$ to capture the frame, transfer it across the bus, and complete neural network inference, the position claim is physically stale by $35\text{ ms}$ before the output tensor reaches the motion controller. The claim can be used only if the model also provides a valid velocity estimate that allows deterministic forward integration. In contrast, a material classification model asserting that a container holds dry aggregate rather than liquid maintains a validity interval spanning hundreds of seconds. The class of a learned part is defined by how rapidly its claim decays against the physical dynamics of the system.

The third axis is checkability, defined as the set of assertions that deterministic software can evaluate on the output before any physical actuator moves. Syntactic and boundary properties are checkable with minimal computation, including output dimensions, numeric ranges, physical units, timestamp age, and deadline compliance ($t_{\text{arrival}} \le t_{\text{deadline}}$). Kinematic and dynamic boundaries can also be verified deterministically, such as ensuring that proposed joint velocities satisfy $|\dot{q}_i| \le \dot{q}_{\text{max}}$ and that proposed end-effector poses lie within the certified reachability envelope. In contrast, semantic correctness, such as whether the proposed target coordinate actually corresponds to the desired workpiece rather than the supporting fixture, cannot be evaluated without duplicating the perception pipeline. Learned parts divide cleanly into those whose dangerous failures fall outside hard physical boundaries, where downstream filters can intercept them, and those whose dangerous failures fall inside nominal operating envelopes, where invalid commands pass undetected into execution.

The fourth axis is authority proximity, which measures the number of deterministic transformations and gating stages between the model output and the motor drives. Two implementations using identical transformer architectures can occupy opposite ends of this axis. In a hierarchical architecture, the transformer outputs a high-level task phase, which is consumed by an analytical trajectory generator and a proportional-integral-derivative controller running at $1000\text{ Hz}$. In an end-to-end architecture, the transformer directly outputs raw actuator current setpoints at $50\text{ Hz}$. The first component has low authority proximity, because its errors are bounded by deterministic motion planners that enforce deceleration limits and obstacle clearance. The second component has high authority proximity, because its output is separated from the physical motor windings only by hardware current limits. As authority proximity increases, the margin for downstream error recovery approaches zero, and the required reliability of the inference execution stack scales accordingly.

Current model families populate specific coordinates across these four axes, establishing distinct hardware and verification requirements as summarized in @tbl-03-model-categories. 

### Vision-Language-Action (VLA) and Foundation Model Architectures {#sec-brain-3-4-vla}

To understand how modern foundation models interface with physical machines, consider the architectural pipeline of Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and multimodal policies (@fig-03-vla-architecture). Unlike classical modular pipelines that separate semantic scene understanding from trajectory optimization, a VLA unifies vision, language comprehension, and low-level motor generation within a single autoregressive transformer backbone:

1. **Multimodal Ingestion and Spatial Tokenization:** High-resolution RGB streams (e.g., $224 \times 224$ or $384 \times 384$ pixels across static overhead and wrist cameras) pass through a visual encoder backbone—typically a Vision Transformer (ViT) such as SigLIP or DINOv2 [@oquab2023dinov2]. The visual encoder partitions each image into regular patches ($14 \times 14$ or $16 \times 16$ pixels), projecting them into linear visual tokens. Natural language task prompts (e.g., `"place the copper terminal into the jig"`) are converted into discrete text tokens via a Byte-Pair Encoding (BPE) or SentencePiece tokenizer. These visual and text tokens are concatenated and passed into a multi-layer transformer backbone—such as PaLM-E (562B) [@driess2023palme], RT-2 (55B) [@brohan2023rt2], or OpenVLA (7B) [@kim2024openvla].

2. **Action Tokenization and Action Spaces:** The fundamental challenge of applying autoregressive language models to robotics is that transformers natively emit discrete categorical tokens over a finite vocabulary, whereas physical actuators require continuous real-valued signals ($u_t \in \mathbb{R}^d$). VLA architectures solve this through two primary paradigms:
   - **Discrete Action Tokenization (Binning):** In models like RT-1 [@brohan2023rt1], RT-2 [@brohan2023rt2], and OpenVLA [@kim2024openvla], continuous 6-DoF or 7-DoF action dimensions (end-effector $\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z, \Delta \text{roll}, \Delta \text{pitch}, \Delta \text{yaw}$, and binary/continuous gripper aperture) are bounded into a defined physical envelope (e.g., $[-0.05\text{ m}, +0.05\text{ m}]$ for linear translation and $[-15^\circ, +15^\circ]$ for rotation) and uniformly quantized into $K$ discrete bins (typically $K = 256$). The model reserves $K$ special tokens in its vocabulary or overwrites least-frequently used text tokens. The transformer autoregressively predicts $d$ sequential action tokens per time-step.
   - **Continuous Latent Action Chunking & Diffusion Heads:** In models like Octo [@octo2024octo], Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) [@zhao2023learning], and Diffusion Policy [@chi2023diffusionpolicy], the transformer backbone serves as a multimodal context encoder whose output representations condition a lightweight generative diffusion head or conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE). The head predicts an entire temporal chunk of continuous actions ($H = 16\text{--}64$ steps over a $320\text{--}1280\text{ ms}$ horizon) in a single inference pass, eliminating single-step Markovian error accumulation and bypassing discrete tokenization artifacts.

3. **The ML Systems Perspective: Roofline Model, Arithmetic Intensity, and the LPDDR5 Memory Wall:**
   To understand why large foundation models cannot directly stabilize physical actuators, we must analyze the hardware limits of deep neural inference from first principles. On any compute platform, the fundamental execution bound is governed by the **Roofline Model**, which relates achievable performance to the **Arithmetic Intensity** ($I$) of the workload:
   $$I = \frac{\text{Operational Work (FLOPs)}}{\text{DRAM Data Movement (Bytes)}} \quad [\text{FLOPs/byte}]$$
   During the multimodal prompt prefill phase (processing visual patch tokens and language instructions), the transformer performs matrix-matrix multiplications ($\text{GEMM}$) across large token batches, exhibiting high arithmetic intensity ($I_{\text{prefill}} \approx \mathcal{O}(S)$, where $S$ is sequence length) that fully saturates parallel tensor systolic arrays.
   
   However, during autoregressive action generation at batch size $B=1$, the transformer executes sequential matrix-vector multiplications ($\text{GEMV}$). For each emitted action token, the processor must read every weight matrix from off-chip DRAM into on-chip registers and SRAM. For a model with $N_{\text{param}}$ parameters stored at precision $b_{\text{param}}$ bytes per parameter (e.g., $b=2$ for FP16, $b=1$ for FP8/INT8, and $b=0.5$ for INT4), generating one token performs $2 N_{\text{param}}$ floating-point operations while transferring $N_{\text{param}} \cdot b_{\text{param}}$ bytes across the memory bus (neglecting small KV-cache overheads for short horizons). The operational arithmetic intensity collapses to a constant:
   $$I_{\text{token}} = \frac{2 N_{\text{param}}}{N_{\text{param}} \cdot b_{\text{param}}} = \frac{2}{b_{\text{param}}} \quad [\text{FLOPs/byte}]$$
   For 16-bit floating-point weights ($b=2$), $I_{\text{token}} = 1.0\text{ FLOP/byte}$. For 8-bit quantized weights ($b=1$), $I_{\text{token}} = 2.0\text{ FLOP/byte}$. For 4-bit quantized weights ($b=0.5$), $I_{\text{token}} = 4.0\text{ FLOP/byte}$.
   
   Now consider a high-performance embedded robotics System-on-Chip (SoC), such as the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin. The platform provides a peak INT8 tensor compute capacity of $P_{\text{compute}} = 275\text{ TOPS}$ ($2.75 \times 10^{14}\text{ OPS/s}$) coupled to a 256-bit LPDDR5 memory subsystem with a theoretical peak bandwidth of $B_{\text{mem}} = 204.8\text{ GB/s}$. The machine balance (the Roofline ridge point where compute units saturate) is:
   $$I_{\text{ridge}} = \frac{P_{\text{compute}}}{B_{\text{mem}}} = \frac{275 \times 10^{12}\text{ OPS/s}}{204.8 \times 10^9\text{ Bytes/s}} \approx 1342.8\text{ OPS/byte}$$
   Because the operational arithmetic intensity of autoregressive decoding ($I_{\text{token}} \le 4.0\text{ OPS/byte}$) is more than two orders of magnitude below the machine balance ridge ($1342.8\text{ OPS/byte}$), **autoregressive VLA action generation is overwhelmingly memory-bandwidth bound**. Over $99.7\%$ of the accelerator's peak tensor compute capacity sits idle, stalled waiting for parameter transfers from DRAM.
   
   Under physical operating conditions, memory bus turnaround overhead, command scheduling, and row buffer conflicts limit sustained DRAM bandwidth to an achievable efficiency of $\eta_{\text{bus}} \approx 0.70$, yielding an effective bandwidth of $B_{\text{achieve}} = \eta_{\text{bus}} \cdot B_{\text{mem}} \approx 143.4\text{ GB/s}$. The minimum physical time required to emit a single token is bounded by the memory transfer time:
   $$t_{\text{token}} = \frac{N_{\text{param}} \cdot b_{\text{param}}}{B_{\text{achieve}}}$$
   
   We can now evaluate the physical consequences of parameter scaling across foundation model scales:
   - **OpenVLA (7B Parameters):** In 8-bit FP8 precision ($b=1$), the weight footprint is $7.0\text{ GB}$. Streaming these weights across the memory bus requires $t_{\text{token}} = \frac{7.0 \times 10^9\text{ bytes}}{143.4 \times 10^9\text{ bytes/s}} \approx 48.8\text{ ms}$ *per token*. Emitting a 7-DoF action vector (7 sequential action tokens: $\Delta x, \Delta y, \Delta z, \Delta \text{roll}, \Delta \text{pitch}, \Delta \text{yaw}$, and gripper) requires $7 \times 48.8\text{ ms} = 341.6\text{ ms}$ of pure DRAM transfer time. Adding visual encoding ($t_{\text{ViT}} \approx 25\text{ ms}$) and multimodal prefill ($t_{\text{prefill}} \approx 15\text{ ms}$) yields a total step latency of $t_{\text{step}} \approx 381.6\text{ ms}$, restricting the closed-loop execution rate to $f_{\text{VLA}} \approx 2.6\text{ Hz}$ (or $3\text{--}5\text{ Hz}$ under aggressive 4-bit quantization).
   - **RT-2 (55B Parameters):** Even with 4-bit INT4 quantization ($b=0.5$), the weight footprint occupies $M_{\text{weights}} = 55 \times 10^9 \times 0.5\text{ bytes} = 27.5\text{ GB}$. Streaming $27.5\text{ GB}$ across the $143.4\text{ GB/s}$ bus takes $t_{\text{token}} = \frac{27.5 \times 10^9\text{ bytes}}{143.4 \times 10^9\text{ bytes/s}} \approx 191.8\text{ ms}$ *per token*. Emitting 7 action tokens requires $7 \times 191.8\text{ ms} \approx 1342.6\text{ ms} = 1.34\text{ s}$ per action step ($f_{\text{VLA}} < 0.75\text{ Hz}$). In 8-bit precision ($55.0\text{ GB}$), the model exceeds the physical $32\text{ GB}$ DRAM capacity of standard edge carriers, triggering OS virtual memory paging across PCIe that degrades latency by another order of magnitude.
   
   This establishes a non-negotiable physical reality: **The LPDDR5 memory bus bandwidth wall permanently confines large autoregressive foundation models to slow deliberative cadences ($1\text{--}5\text{ Hz}$) on edge silicon.**
   
   To bypass this memory bottleneck, generative diffusion policies and Action Chunking with Transformers (ACT) decouple context encoding from action generation. Instead of streaming billions of parameters token by token, a lightweight policy head ($50\text{M--}150\text{M}$ parameters, requiring $<300\text{ MB}$ DRAM) is evaluated over a continuous action space, predicting an entire chunk of $H=16\text{--}64$ future waypoints in a single forward or denoising pass ($30\text{--}50\text{ ms}$). This amortizes multimodal deliberation over multi-hundred-millisecond horizons, achieving an effective proposal generation rate of $30\text{--}50\text{ Hz}$.

4. **The Proposal–Permission Boundary in Dual-Brain Hardware:**
   Because VLA inference is high-latency ($200\text{--}1300\text{ ms}$), memory-bound, and susceptible to semantic hallucination, a learned foundation model must never possess direct register write authority to motor inverters. Instead, the VLA operates strictly as an **unprivileged proposal engine** ($\mathcal{H}_{\text{brain}}$) [@sha2001using; @alshiekh2018safe].
   
   In the **Physical AI Kit (Arduino UNO Q reference architecture)**, this separation is enforced in hardware:
   - The Linux MPU (ARM Cortex-A) runs the memory-bandwidth-bound VLA, generative diffusion planner, or ROS 2 navigation stack, asynchronously generating unprivileged candidate trajectory chunks ($p_t$).
   - The bare-metal MCU (STM32 ARM Cortex-M) runs the hard real-time safety supervisor ($\mathcal{H}_{\text{nervous}}$) at $1000\text{ Hz}$ from deterministic, zero-wait-state on-chip SRAM.
   - Proposals cross the hardware isolation boundary via RPMSG mailboxes backed by shared SRAM, carrying monotonic sequence IDs, capture timestamps, and validity lease durations ($\tau_{\text{lease}}$).
   - The MCU evaluates Control Barrier Functions ($h(x) \ge 0$) and dynamic stopping envelopes ($d_{\text{stop}} \le D_{\text{clear}}$) at $1\text{ ms}$ intervals before committing pulse-width modulation (PWM) gate drive signals ($u_t$) to actuator inverter bridges. If the MPU stalls behind the memory bus or an intent lease expires, the MCU trips its independent countdown watchdog ($\tau_{\text{watchdog}} \le 10\text{ ms}$) and triggers a deterministic safe-stop refusal ($\bot$).

![**Vision-Language-Action (VLA) Model Architecture, Tokenization Pipeline, and Proposal–Permission Interfacing.** (1) Multi-camera RGB streams (overhead and wrist) and natural language task prompts are tokenized into visual patch tokens via ViT backbones and text tokens via BPE tokenizers. (2) A 7B–55B autoregressive transformer backbone fusses multimodal tokens, streaming multi-gigabyte weight tensors across the memory bus at 3–5 Hz on edge accelerators. (3) Actions are emitted either as discrete quantized tokens (Paradigm A: RT-2 / OpenVLA 256-bin discretization) or continuous latent conditioning vectors driving multi-step action chunking diffusion heads (Paradigm B: Octo / ACT). (4) Downstream, candidate action chunks pass across the hardware isolation boundary via RPMSG/PCIe DMA into a bare-metal 1 kHz microcontroller running Control Barrier Function QP filters that evaluate dynamic stopping clearance before motor register commits.](figures/fig03_vla_architecture.svg){#fig-03-vla-architecture fig-pos="t" width=95%}

|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
