: **Architectural and Systems Trade-Offs across Learned Component Classes.** Comparison of primary learned model families deployed in embodied systems, detailing physical claims, memory and compute resource footprints on embedded edge accelerators, physical validity horizons, and the deterministic supervisory interceptors required before commands reach actuator hardware. {#tbl-03-model-categories}

When evaluating a newly proposed learned component, the engineer does not need to analyze its neural network topology to determine its systems requirements. Locating the component on the four axes of physical claim, validity interval, checkability, and authority proximity specifies the necessary compute deadlines, the required bus bandwidth, the failure interceptors, and the fallback behaviors of the host machine. Regardless of where a learned part sits across these four dimensions, its output fundamentally differs from deterministic software output, because it is never a certified truth, but a sample drawn from an underlying distribution.
<!-- END -->

## Outputs as Distributions {#sec-brain-3-5}

<!-- SECTION 3.5 -->
<!-- claim: A model returns a distribution, and the number it reports as confidence usually does not mean what it appears to mean. -->
<!-- covers: Distinguish a point estimate, an unnormalized score, a normalized class score, a sample, and a predictive distribution; deployment code must not call all five “confidence.” -->
<!-- covers: Define the event to which confidence refers, including its time horizon and success criterion, before testing calibration. -->
<!-- covers: Compute empirical success frequency within score bins and retain the sample count in each bin so that a sparse bin is not mistaken for reliable calibration. -->
<!-- covers: Show that calibration is population-level evidence and does not certify the next individual output. -->
<!-- covers: Use a risk-coverage curve to choose an abstention threshold, and require a downstream response that remains safe when the model abstains. -->
<!-- covers: Explain why distribution shift can invalidate an offline calibration result while providing no immediate correctness label at runtime. -->
<!-- GROUNDING: number — reported confidence against measured frequency of being right -->
<!-- FIGURE: A two-panel empirical plot must SHOW a model whose reported scores are miscalibrated and how lowering coverage through abstention changes the observed error rate. -->
<!-- DERIVE: Derive calibration error from reported scores and observed frequencies, including bin counts; do not infer calibrated probability from softmax normalization. -->

<!-- BEGIN -->
Deployment interfaces frequently collapse distinct mathematical artifacts into a single scalar labeled confidence. A deterministic point estimate is a single coordinate in the output space, such as an end-effector target $\hat{y} \in \mathbb{R}^3$. An unnormalized logit $z_k \in \mathbb{R}$ represents the raw activation energy of an output unit prior to normalization. A normalized class score $p_k = \exp(z_k) / \sum_j \exp(z_j)$ maps logits onto a unit simplex so that the values sum to one, yet this exponentiation is a mathematical property of the softmax function rather than an empirical measure of physical success. A sample $\tilde{y} \sim p(y \mid x)$ is a single realization drawn from an internal stochastic process, such as a denoising step in a diffusion policy or a token roll-out in an autoregressive model. A predictive distribution $p(y \mid x)$ characterizes the entire density over the action envelope, providing moments, variances, or multimodal bounds. When execution software treats all five outputs interchangeably as confidence, it mistakes mathematical range normalization for physical certainty.[^fn_lipschitz_calibration]

To determine whether a reported scalar corresponds to reality, an engineering specification must define the physical event, its time horizon, and its success criterion before collecting validation data. In machine control, a statement that a vision model is ninety percent confident has no operational meaning without an explicit physical contract. For an autonomous transport vehicle detecting a dock boundary, the target event is not the emission of a bounding box, but the requirement that the estimated boundary remains within $\pm 2.0\text{ cm}$ of the physical edge across the entire $200\text{ ms}$ validity interval. If the model emits an output score of $0.90$, calibration demands testing whether ninety out of one hundred instances of that score result in an edge estimate that satisfies the geometric tolerance over that exact time window. Without an explicit physical criterion and a bounded duration, confidence numbers measure only internal statistical artifacts.

The alignment between reported scores and empirical success is evaluated through **calibration**, which measures the difference between predicted confidence and observed accuracy across discrete confidence intervals. Consider an analytical example of a perception policy evaluated on $N = 10000$ validation cycles divided into $M = 5$ confidence bins of width $0.20$. Let $B_m$ denote the set of sample indices whose predicted confidence $\hat{p}_i$ falls in the interval $((m-1)/M, m/M]$. In the highest bin $B_5$, spanning scores from $0.80$ to $1.00$, the model processes $|B_5| = 5000$ frames with an average predicted confidence $\text{conf}(B_5) = \frac{1}{|B_5|} \sum_{i \in B_5} \hat{p}_i = 0.910$. The physical accuracy measured across those frames is $\text{acc}(B_5) = \frac{1}{|B_5|} \sum_{i \in B_5} y_i = 0.720$, where $y_i = 1$ if the physical tracking tolerance was met and $0$ otherwise, leaving a calibration error of $|0.910 - 0.720| = 0.190$. In bin $B_4$, covering scores from $0.60$ to $0.80$, $|B_4| = 3000$ frames yield an average confidence of $0.710$ and an observed accuracy of $0.550$, producing an error of $0.160$. In bin $B_3$, with scores from $0.40$ to $0.60$, $|B_3| = 1500$ frames yield an average confidence of $0.510$ and an accuracy of $0.400$, an error of $0.110$. In bin $B_2$, covering scores from $0.20$ to $0.40$, $|B_2| = 450$ frames produce an average confidence of $0.310$ and an accuracy of $0.240$, an error of $0.070$. In the lowest bin $B_1$, covering scores from $0.00$ to $0.20$, $|B_1| = 50$ frames produce an average confidence of $0.140$ and an observed accuracy of $0.140$, yielding an apparent error of $0.000$.

The overall quality of the distribution is summarized by the **expected calibration error**, which weights each bin's absolute gap by its empirical sample fraction. The metric is defined as
$$\text{ECE} = \sum_{m=1}^M \frac{|B_m|}{N} |\text{acc}(B_m) - \text{conf}(B_m)|.$$
Substituting the analytical validation values yields
$$\begin{aligned}
\text{ECE} = \frac{50}{10000}(0.000) &+ \frac{450}{10000}(0.070) + \frac{1500}{10000}(0.110) \\
&+ \frac{3000}{10000}(0.160) + \frac{5000}{10000}(0.190),
\end{aligned}$$
which evaluates to $0.00000 + 0.00315 + 0.01650 + 0.04800 + 0.09500 = 0.16265$, or $16.27\text{ percent}$. Recording the sample count $|B_m|$ alongside the score gap is an absolute operational requirement. In bin $B_1$, the calibration gap is zero, creating the illusion of perfect calibration in low-confidence regimes. However, because $B_1$ contains only 50 samples out of 10000, a single unexpected failure would change its empirical accuracy from $14.0\text{ percent}$ down to $12.0\text{ percent}$, introducing an instantaneous gap of $0.020$. An unpopulated bin cannot provide statistical evidence of reliable calibration.

Even when a component demonstrates low expected calibration error across an offline test benchmark, calibration remains an aggregate property of a dataset rather than an operational certificate for the next step. If a trajectory model is calibrated at a confidence score of $0.90$, exactly ten out of every one hundred execution steps will produce an invalid trajectory. The downstream tracking loop receives an individual numerical vector on the current cycle, with no attached indication of whether that vector belongs to the ninety successful executions or the ten failures. In a data center pipeline, a ten-percent failure rate causes an occasional retry or a dropped connection. In a physical machine, if an articulated arm executes an unvalidated trajectory command at $1.5\text{ m/s}$, the linkage strikes a structural constraint long before population averages can correct the trajectory.

To protect the machine from low-confidence actions, the nervous system employs selective execution through an abstention threshold $\tau$. When the model's reported score $\hat{p}_i$ falls below $\tau$, the execution stack rejects the learned proposal and invokes a deterministic fallback controller. The operational trade-off is governed by a **risk-coverage curve**, where coverage $C(\tau)$ represents the proportion of cycles handled by the learned policy,
$$C(\tau) = \frac{1}{N} \sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{I}(\hat{p}_i \ge \tau),$$
and selective risk $R(\tau)$ represents the empirical error rate among those accepted proposals,
$$R(\tau) = \frac{\sum_{i=1}^N (1 - y_i) \cdot \mathbb{I}(\hat{p}_i \ge \tau)}{\sum_{i=1}^N \mathbb{I}(\hat{p}_i \ge \tau)}.$$
In our analytical example, setting an abstention threshold at $\tau = 0.80$ restricts the policy to predictions in bin $B_5$. This choice reduces coverage to $C(0.80) = 5000 / 10000 = 50.0\text{ percent}$, while reducing the operational error rate from the unconstrained baseline of $40.35\text{ percent}$ down to $28.0\text{ percent}$. Setting an abstention threshold, however, solves only half of the systems problem. The machine must have a fallback policy that remains physically safe when the learned component abstains. If a mobile base traveling at $2.0\text{ m/s}$ enters an unmodeled visual condition and drops its steering confidence to $0.45$, abstaining from action cannot mean freezing the steering angle. The nervous system must command a controlled deceleration that halts the vehicle within the remaining sensor line of sight.

Every calibration metric and risk-coverage threshold established during development assumes that the runtime environment mirrors the training distribution. In physical deployment, optical dust on a lens, sensor thermal drift, shifting sunlight, or mechanical backlash shift the input distribution away from the validation baseline. When distribution shift occurs, the model's internal representations diverge, and the offline calibration curve becomes invalid. The physical machine receives no ground-truth correctness labels during operation, observing only its incoming sensor stream and the model's miscalibrated outputs. Under severe distribution shift, a vision model can continue to output confidence scores above $0.95$ while its empirical success rate falls to zero. The runtime system has no internal mechanism to detect this divergence from the output scores alone.

The systematic breakdown of confidence calibration across operational environments follows distinct distribution shift regimes, as quantified in @tbl-03-calibration-degradation. Under nominal in-distribution conditions, expected calibration error remains tightly bounded ($\text{ECE} \le 0.035$), allowing selective execution thresholds to suppress the bulk of residual errors. Under near-out-of-distribution (near-OOD) covariate shift—such as specular glare or lens droplets—the model exhibits severe overconfidence, inflating calibration error ($\Delta \text{ECE} = +0.370$) and necessitating statistical embedding monitors to trigger velocity clamps. Under far-OOD semantic shifts or progressive sensor drift, reported confidence decouples entirely from physical success, demanding immediate proposal refusal and deterministic safe-stop braking.

| Distribution Shift Regime | Physical & Environmental Trigger | Nominal Conf. vs Measured Acc. ($\text{conf} \text{ vs } \text{acc}$) | Calibration Gap ($\Delta \text{ECE}$) | Runtime Statistical Signal | Downstream Gating & Deterministic Fallback |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **In-Distribution** (Nominal Baseline) | Clean optics, structured laboratory lighting, nominal workpiece textures | $\text{conf}=0.910, \, \text{acc}=0.885$ | $\text{ECE} \le 0.035$ (Calibrated) | Normalized softmax entropy within nominal envelope | Full autonomous execution permitted; nominal velocity profiles |
| **Near-OOD Shift** (Covariate Shift) | Specular reflections, lens water droplets, dynamic shadow transitions | $\text{conf}=0.890, \, \text{acc}=0.520$ | $\Delta \text{ECE} = +0.370$ (Overconfident) | Embedding Mahalanobis distance $D_M \ge 3.0\sigma$; feature norm spike | Selective abstention triggered: clamp maximum velocity to $v_{\text{safe}}$, initiate exploratory tactile probing |
| **Far-OOD Shift** (Semantic Shift) | Uncataloged deformable obstacles, human limb intrusion into workspace | $\text{conf}=0.780, \, \text{acc}=0.080$ | $\Delta \text{ECE} = +0.700$ (Pathological) | Energy-score threshold breach ($E(x) \ge E_{\text{thresh}}$); ensemble variance spike | Immediate proposal refusal: hold current state, engage controlled braking ($a_{\text{max}}$) |
| **Sensor Degradation** (Concept / Hardware Shift) | Photodetector thermal noise ($>75^\circ\text{C}$), focal blur from vibration, mechanical backlash | $\text{conf}=0.840, \, \text{acc}=0.310$ | $\Delta \text{ECE} = +0.530$ (Silent failure) | Rolling residual innovation covariance divergence in state estimator | Trigger operational downgrade; notify fleet telemetry; restrict kinematics to certified safe envelope |

: **Expected Calibration Error (ECE) and Failure Profiles across Distribution Shift Regimes.** Quantitative breakdown of nominal model confidence versus empirical physical task success rates, calibration error degradation, statistical runtime indicators, and deterministic supervisory actions under progressive environmental and sensor anomalies. {#tbl-03-calibration-degradation}

Because learned components cannot verify their own outputs or signal when their calibration has failed, authority over physical movement cannot rest with the model's internal confidence. Every output distribution must be verified, bounded, and cross-checked against deterministic constraints before reaching an actuator. Evaluating these distributions, computing abstention thresholds, and maintaining fallback buffers requires dedicated memory bandwidth, bus transfers, and compute cycles on every tick of the execution clock.
<!-- END -->

## The Cost of Inference {#sec-brain-3-6}

<!-- SECTION 3.6 -->
<!-- claim: Every property of a learned part is a withdrawal from one of the five limits. -->
<!-- covers: Define the inference timing boundary from input-ready to output-ready, including device synchronization and asynchronous accelerator completion. -->
<!-- covers: Measure warm, cold, isolated, contended, and thermally throttled runs rather than reporting one benchmark average. -->
<!-- covers: Report the latency distribution with sample count, $P_{50}$, relevant tail percentiles, maximum observed value, and the body limit against which each is judged. -->
<!-- covers: Decompose peak memory into weights, activations, retained context, allocator overhead, and copies introduced at component boundaries. -->
<!-- covers: Convert bytes transferred per inference and invocation rate into sustained bandwidth, then identify the sensors, trackers, and enforcer competing for that bandwidth. -->
<!-- covers: Integrate measured power over an inference to obtain energy, then show how invocation rate creates sustained heat and how throttling feeds back into latency. -->
<!-- covers: Map every measurement to a remaining @sec-body margin and label analytical extrapolations separately from target-device measurements. -->
<!-- GROUNDING: number — latency, footprint, bandwidth, and heat, each as a draw on @sec-body -->
<!-- FIGURE: A target-device latency CDF under isolated, contended, and thermally throttled runs must SHOW how the same model consumes different fractions of the body’s freshness limit. -->
<!-- DERIVE: Derive bandwidth from bytes per invocation and rate, energy from the power trace, and sustained thermal draw from energy and duty cycle rather than using vendor throughput as a proxy. -->

<!-- BEGIN -->
In an embodied machine, deep neural inference executes on dedicated edge accelerator modules (@fig-03-jetson-orin), where neural processing units, unified DRAM, and high-throughput peripheral interfaces are constrained by tight thermal and electrical power envelopes. Every property of a learned part is a withdrawal from one of the five physical limits established in @sec-body. In disembodied software benchmarks, an inference measurement records the execution duration of a forward pass across an isolated accelerator, omitting host scheduling, tensor serialization, and device synchronization. In Physical AI, the inference timing boundary spans from the exact instant an input observation is committed to memory and ready for consumption (input-ready) to the instant the resulting action proposal is fully written into host-accessible memory and certified for execution (output-ready). This boundary includes sensor preprocessing, Direct Memory Access transfers across the system bus, accelerator kernel launches, intermediate synchronization barriers, and the transfer of output tensors back to the control processor. Because modern neural accelerators execute asynchronously relative to the host CPU, an inference is not complete when the host finishes enqueuing command buffers. It completes only when the accelerator signals hardware completion and all write buffers are flushed.

![**Embedded Robotic Edge AI Accelerator (NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin).** A physical edge compute carrier board showing the multi-core Ampere GPU/Tensor Core and ARM CPU system-on-chip beneath an active finned aluminum heat sink and fan assembly, flanked by high-speed MIPI CSI-2 camera ribbon connectors, PCIe Gen4 expansion, multi-gigabit Ethernet, and power delivery regulation circuitry. The physical architecture highlights the shared unified memory bus ($2048\text{-bit}$ LPDDR5), where deep neural network parameter streaming and DMA sensor ingest compete for memory bandwidth, and where electrical power dissipation ($15\text{--}60\text{ W}$) governs thermal throttling boundaries during real-time robotic control. (Photograph by Auledas, CC BY 4.0).](figures/fig03_real_jetson_orin.png){#fig-03-jetson-orin fig-pos="t" width=85%}

Evaluating this latency requires testing across five operational regimes, spanning warm, cold, isolated, contended, and thermally throttled execution. Reporting a single average execution time hides the operational tail that governs physical safety. In an analytical example on an embedded System-on-Chip (SoC) operating an articulated arm with a physical freshness limit of $\tau_{\text{world}} = 100\text{ ms}$, we evaluate $N = 10{,}000$ consecutive inference cycles of a vision-guided policy. Under warm, isolated conditions with no background traffic, the policy achieves a median latency of $P_{50} = 24.2\text{ ms}$, a tail latency of $P_{99} = 28.6\text{ ms}$, and a maximum observed latency of $31.4\text{ ms}$. This isolated profile consumes less than a third of the freshness budget. In contrast, a cold invocation exhibits a latency spike of $412.0\text{ ms}$ due to weight paging from secondary storage, memory allocator initialization, and cache warm-up, exceeding the physical safety deadline by more than a factor of four before the first physical movement begins.

When the model executes in a contended environment alongside active system processes, shared hardware resources distort this distribution. In our analytical example, running the policy concurrently with sensor ingest DMA channels, real-time SLAM updates, and safety monitor checks shifts the median latency to $P_{50} = 38.5\text{ ms}$, inflates the tail latency to $P_{99} = 88.2\text{ ms}$, and produces a maximum observed latency of $114.6\text{ ms}$. Under these contended conditions, $0.4\text{ percent}$ of all cycles cross the $100\text{ ms}$ freshness wall. At a payload speed of $1.5\text{ m/s}$, a single $114.6\text{ ms}$ tail event carries the robot $17.2\text{ cm}$ past the physical state where the camera frame was captured. The resulting motion command arrives at the actuators after physical reality has diverged from the model's internal representation.

The second withdrawal is memory footprint, budgeted across static model parameters, intermediate activation tensors, retained temporal context, memory allocator overhead, and boundary copy buffers. In our analytical example of a 450-million-parameter policy stored in 16-bit floating-point format, the static weights occupy $450 \times 10^6 \times 2\text{ bytes} = 900\text{ MB}$. Peak intermediate activation tensors during the forward pass require $340\text{ MB}$. Retaining a 16-frame temporal context of past observations consumes $180\text{ MB}$. Dynamic memory allocator fragmentation and runtime execution metadata add $120\text{ MB}$. Finally, zero-copy driver fallbacks and inter-process communication buffers introduce $110\text{ MB}$ of memory duplication across component boundaries. The resulting peak memory consumption totals $900 + 340 + 180 + 120 + 110 = 1650\text{ MB}$ ($1.65\text{ GB}$). On an embedded compute platform with a $4.0\text{ GB}$ DRAM allocation for autonomy, this single component consumes $41.25\text{ percent}$ of total system memory, leaving $2.35\text{ GB}$ for the operating system kernel, point cloud maps, and the real-time safety supervisor.

This memory footprint translates directly into sustained bus bandwidth when the model executes at a fixed invocation rate. In our analytical example, each forward pass streams $900\text{ MB}$ of weights from DRAM, reads and writes $520\text{ MB}$ of layer activations, and writes the output action tensors, generating $1.42\text{ GB}$ of DRAM traffic per inference. Invoking the policy at an operational rate of $20\text{ Hz}$ generates a continuous memory bandwidth demand of $1.42\text{ GB} \times 20\text{ s}^{-1} = 28.4\text{ GB/s}$. On an SoC with a theoretical peak memory bandwidth of $68.0\text{ GB/s}$ and an empirical saturation ceiling of $54.4\text{ GB/s}$ ($80\text{ percent}$ of peak), the neural policy competes directly with peripheral traffic. Dual stereo cameras streaming raw frames at $60\text{ Hz}$ demand $4.8\text{ GB/s}$, 3D LiDAR point cloud ingest requires $3.2\text{ GB/s}$, state estimation consumes $2.6\text{ GB/s}$, and the 1000 Hz safety enforcer requires $1.4\text{ GB/s}$. Total sustained traffic reaches $40.4\text{ GB/s}$, which represents $74.3\text{ percent}$ of the achievable bus ceiling. During transient memory access bursts where aggregate traffic approaches saturation, memory controller arbitration stalls delay accelerator access, directly generating the $P_{99}$ latency tail.[^fn_npu_memory_wall]

Integrating the measured electrical power trace over the duration of an inference yields the energy cost per action proposal, which governs sustained thermal dissipation. In our analytical example, the hardware draws $4.5\text{ W}$ at idle and $28.0\text{ W}$ during active compute. Across the nominal $38.5\text{ ms}$ execution window, each inference consumes $E_{\text{infer}} = 28.0\text{ W} \times 0.0385\text{ s} = 1.078\text{ J}$ of electrical energy. Invoking the policy at $20\text{ Hz}$ keeps the accelerator active for $0.770\text{ s}$ out of every second, representing a $77.0\text{ percent}$ duty cycle. The resulting continuous thermal dissipation is $28.0\text{ W} \times 0.770 + 4.5\text{ W} \times 0.230 = 22.60\text{ W}$. In a sealed, passively cooled enclosure dimensioned for a steady-state dissipation limit of $15.0\text{ W}$, thermal energy accumulates at an unmanaged rate of $7.60\text{ J/s}$. Within $90\text{ seconds}$, silicon junction temperature exceeds the $85^\circ\text{C}$ threshold, triggering Dynamic Voltage and Frequency Scaling (DVFS). Under thermal throttling, accelerator clock frequencies drop by half, stretching the median execution time to $54.0\text{ ms}$, expanding the $P_{99}$ latency to $142.8\text{ ms}$, and forcing the real-time supervisor to reject late proposals on almost every cycle.

This thermal and memory contention reality explains why physical AI systems enforce heterogeneous dual-brain hardware partitioning. On the host application processor (Linux MPU), deep neural networks draw substantial electrical power ($15\text{--}50\text{ W}$ on high-performance SoCs or $2\text{--}5\text{ W}$ on embedded boards like the Arduino UNO Q), contend for shared DRAM bandwidth, and suffer operating system thread preemption and thermal clock throttling. In sharp contrast, the deterministic safety referee (bare-metal MCU) operates at sub-watt power levels ($<100\text{ mW}$), executing its $1000\text{ Hz}$ Control Barrier Function loops directly out of zero-wait-state Tightly Coupled Memory (TCM) or on-chip SRAM. Because the MCU does not touch external DRAM and runs without an asynchronous operating system kernel, its worst-case execution time (WCET) remains deterministically bounded below $1.0\text{ ms}$ with sub-microsecond jitter, ensuring that motor safety barriers are evaluated unconditionally even when the neural MPU throttles or stalls.

Every property of a learned model represents an explicit deduction from the physical margins established in @sec-body. Adding attention layers, expanding the observation history, or increasing parameter precision draws down the remaining reserves of time, memory capacity, bus bandwidth, battery energy, and thermal headroom. When these physical withdrawals exceed available capacity, the component degrades the closed-loop stability of the entire machine. When the physical margins are preserved, the model delivers candidate actions within the limits the machine can tolerate. When a learned component fails, however, its failure modes differ fundamentally from conventional software faults. They produce valid tensor shapes, execute without system exceptions, and remain entirely invisible to the runtime environment that hosts them.
<!-- END -->

## How Learned Parts Fail {#sec-brain-3-7}

<!-- SECTION 3.7 -->
<!-- claim: The failure modes of a learned component are few, well understood, and mostly undetectable at runtime. -->
<!-- covers: Replace the claim that failures are “few” with a bounded taxonomy covering incorrect outputs, misleading uncertainty, deployment shift, and missed runtime contracts. -->
<!-- covers: Treat an out-of-distribution score as an imperfect statistical signal whose false-accept rate must be measured on named near- and far-shift cases. -->
<!-- covers: Show that a calibration or abstention monitor can flag some risky outputs but cannot determine semantic correctness without a timely reference label. -->
<!-- covers: Detect deployment drift over a population and time window, while stating that such a detector usually cannot adjudicate the current action. -->
<!-- covers: Detect deadline, range, freshness, and missing-output failures deterministically from timestamps and interface checks, then expire or refuse the proposal. -->
<!-- covers: Record the input provenance, model version, output, monitor result, timing, and disposition needed to reconstruct every detected or later-discovered failure. -->
<!-- GROUNDING: failure — four failure modes, each with its detector or the absence of one -->
<!-- DERIVE: Derive runtime detectability by identifying what observable evidence exists before actuation for each failure class; remove “mostly undetectable” unless the resulting taxonomy supports it. -->

<!-- BEGIN -->
A conventional software component fails by throwing an exception, dereferencing a null pointer, or deadlocking a thread. A learned model fails by emitting numbers that satisfy every type signature and tensor dimension while commanding an impossible or destructive physical state. Rather than treating these failures as an unbounded collection of unpredictable behaviors, an engineer budgets for a bounded taxonomy of four distinct failure classes. These comprise missed runtime contracts, incorrect outputs, misleading uncertainty, and deployment shift. Each class presents a different observable signature to the host system, and each imposes a different limit on what can be detected before energy reaches the physical plant.

The first class consists of missed runtime contracts, where the failure manifests in temporal or structural metadata rather than the numerical values inside the tensor. These faults include deadline misses, stale inputs, missing outputs, non-finite values such as floating-point overflows or divisions by zero resulting in NaN tokens, and array shape mismatches. In an analytical example where an inference runtime is budgeted for a $50\text{ ms}$ deadline, a hardware stall that delays output delivery to $52\text{ ms}$ violates the timing contract. These failures are fully and deterministically detectable before actuation. A non-blocking watchdog timer, an interface schema validator, and a timestamp freshness check running on the host CPU can verify tensor dimensions, inspect every float for validity, and check arrival times against the hardware clock within $10\text{ }\mu\text{s}$. If the candidate output fails any check, the host runtime discards the proposal, expires the stale command, and executes a deterministic fallback.

The second class encompasses incorrect outputs, where a syntactically pristine tensor commands an erroneous or destructive physical action. The model generates a torque proposal of $18.4\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$ when the joint configuration demands $2.1\text{ N}\cdot\text{m}$, or predicts a clear trajectory straight through a transparent acrylic barrier. The tensor arrives within its $50\text{ ms}$ deadline, passes all dimension and range checks, and contains strictly finite numbers. At the moment of inference, this failure is entirely undetectable by the model execution framework. The runtime environment cannot evaluate semantic correctness because doing so requires a reference label, which does not exist in an operational setting. The host system possesses no internal oracle to determine whether an action proposal reflects an optimal trajectory or a catastrophic hallucination until the physical body interacts with its environment.

The third class comprises misleading uncertainty and out-of-distribution inputs, where the model encounters observation states outside its training support yet generates high-confidence, erroneous outputs. An engineer can attach a statistical monitor, such as an embedding-space Mahalanobis distance metric, an ensemble variance estimator, or a density estimator, to score whether an observation diverges from nominal training data. However, an out-of-distribution score is an imperfect statistical signal rather than a hard deterministic barrier. The detector operates with an unavoidable trade-off between its false-alarm rate and its false-accept rate. In an analytical evaluation on a navigation policy, a density monitor calibrated for a $1.0\text{ percent}$ false-alarm rate on nominal inputs exhibits a false-accept rate below $0.1\text{ percent}$ on far-shift cases, such as complete sensor occlusion or severe lens distortion. On near-shift cases, such as subtle wet pavement reflections or novel lighting angles that degrade visual feature tracking, the false-accept rate rises to $34.2\text{ percent}$. Abstention monitors and temperature calibration can scale or suppress predictions when confidence metrics register low values, but they cannot verify whether a high-confidence prediction is semantically correct.

The fourth class involves deployment shift, where the distribution of operating conditions drifts gradually away from the training distribution across hours, days, or operational fleets. This drift arises from mechanical wear in gearboxes, sensor calibration degradation from thermal cycling, lens fouling from environmental dust, or seasonal variations in ambient illumination. At the level of an individual inference at time $t$, this failure mode is undetectable because each single observation and proposed action appears statistically plausible within typical operating limits. Detection requires accumulating aggregate statistics over a population of inferences and an extended temporal window, such as tracking the drift in mean feature activations, actuation energy histograms, or closed-loop state tracking error residuals across a ten-minute rolling window. While an aggregate drift monitor successfully flags that the machine is operating in a degraded regime and prompts an operational downgrade or maintenance alert, it operates at macroscopic timescales and cannot adjudicate whether the specific action proposal on the current $20\text{ Hz}$ cycle is safe to execute.

Because semantic correctness and instantaneous distributional shifts remain undetectable prior to actuation, the host architecture must treat every inference as an unverified proposal and record the provenance needed to analyze failures retrospectively. When an undetected model failure leads to a trajectory divergence or an intervention by a downstream governor, post-incident reconstruction requires an exact record of the execution context. The runtime logging pipeline captures the input sensor frames with their hardware capture timestamps, the model version hash and parameter checkpoint identifier, the raw unclipped output tensors, all intermediate monitor scores, the end-to-end execution latency, and the final disposition chosen by downstream arbitration logic. Preserving this telemetry across a rolling ring buffer allows engineers to replay the precise state sequence in simulation, isolate whether a failure stemmed from input corruption, model misgeneralization, or runtime resource contention, and audit the interaction without relying on model introspection.

These four failure modes establish what a learned model can and cannot guarantee to the machine that contains it. The model can provide candidate actions that discover effective behaviors across high-dimensional sensor spaces, but it cannot guarantee semantic correctness, cannot reliably verify its own validity under novel inputs, and cannot be trusted with unilateral authority over physical actuation. Protecting the physical machine requires placing the learned model within a pipeline of distinct functional stages, where each boundary enforces specific invariant contracts, translates unverified representations into bounded physical quantities, and prevents an unmonitored tensor from directly driving an actuator.
<!-- END -->

## The Five Handoffs {#sec-brain-3-8}

<!-- SECTION 3.8 -->
<!-- claim: Observe, estimate, intend, plan, enforce. Five things get handed along, each boundary exists because the sender cannot supply what the receiver needs, and only the last may command energy. -->
<!-- covers: Observe hands over timestamped evidence with provenance and validity metadata, not an interpretation of what the world contains. -->
<!-- covers: Estimate hands over a state or belief with uncertainty and age, because observations do not state system state directly. -->
<!-- covers: Intend hands over a goal with issuer, scope, priority, and expiration, because a state does not choose a goal and a once-valid objective must not become permanent. -->
<!-- covers: Plan hands over a time-indexed candidate with feasibility assumptions and a validity horizon, because a goal does not supply a feasible trajectory. -->
<!-- covers: Enforce hands over either an allowed bounded command or an explicit refusal with a reason, because a trajectory does not grant permission; only this output may enter the command path. -->
<!-- covers: Derive each boundary from the rejection test it makes possible: an invalid timestamp refused at Observe, an over-age estimate refused before Intend, an expired intent refused before Planning, an infeasible plan refused without relitigating the goal, and a feasible proposal clipped or refused at the current physical limit. -->
<!-- covers: Carry age, uncertainty, and validity metadata forward rather than stripping them when the primary value crosses an interface. -->
<!-- covers: Treat the five names as system functions rather than as five models or processes, and distinguish logical separation from deployment placement: an end-to-end policy may span several functions, and what it costs is the inspection point, the expiry, and the refusal that the collapsed contract used to provide. -->
<!-- covers: Compress the chain into what is at stake at each step, because this is the shape Part III follows: a prediction is not a decision, a decision is not a command, and a command is not yet an action. Perception and memory produce predictions, intent produces a decision, planning produces a candidate command, and only enforcement turns one into an action. -->
<!-- GROUNDING: mechanism — five handoffs, each named by what it produces and by the rejection test its boundary makes possible -->
<!-- FIGURE: The canonical chain must SHOW each named handoff and its artifact, with dashed proposal paths becoming a solid allowed-command path only after Enforce and with refusals terminating visibly. A second register draws the same machine as one end-to-end policy, with the lost inspection points marked. -->
<!-- DERIVE: Derive the chain from the distinct information transformation and rejection test at each boundary; collapsing stages does not automatically remove refusal unless the lost test is identified. -->

<!-- BEGIN -->
Every machine with learned components structures its execution around five discrete handoffs: observe, estimate, intend, plan, and enforce (@fig-03-five-handoffs). Five distinct artifacts move along this chain, each boundary exists because the sending stage cannot supply the guarantees the receiving stage requires, and only the final handoff is permitted to command physical energy. Placing a learned model inside this sequence does not alter the underlying information dependencies. A neural network may generate representations, choose candidate goals, or interpolate trajectories, but it cannot convert an ungrounded sensory voltage into a physical action without crossing these five functional boundaries.

The first handoff, Observe, transfers timestamped sensory evidence with explicit provenance and hardware validity metadata, rather than an interpretation of what the environment contains. A monochrome camera frame, a time-of-flight depth array, or a joint encoder reading is not a statement about physical objects. It is a record of energy transduced at a specific physical detector during a bounded exposure interval. The contract at this boundary demands an immutable capture timestamp from a monotonic hardware clock, a sensor identifier, and hardware error flags indicating optical saturation or dropped packets. This boundary enables an immediate rejection test. If a camera frame arrives with a desynchronized timestamp, a corrupted CRC checksum, or a transport delay exceeding an analytical budget of $15\text{ ms}$, the observation is rejected before consuming memory bandwidth or polluting downstream pipelines with stale evidence.

The second handoff, Estimate, converts raw observation streams into a metric state belief accompanied by explicit uncertainty bounds and an age metric, because raw observations never state system state directly. A single camera image contains no direct measurement of linear velocity, mass distribution, or occluded geometry. The estimation stage fuses multi-modal observations across time into spatial coordinates, velocity vectors, and covariance matrices defined within a rigid reference frame. The boundary contract requires that every state estimate carry the elapsed time since sensor integration and the uncertainty covariance derived from measurement noise. This interface provides the second rejection test. If visual tracking fails or if latency pushes the estimate age beyond an analytical threshold of $50\text{ ms}$, the downstream decision logic refuses the state before attempting to evaluate a goal against an ungrounded belief.

The third handoff, Intend, transfers a bounded operational goal carrying an authorized issuer, a spatial scope, a priority level, and an explicit expiration timestamp, because an estimated state does not select a task. Knowing that an obstacle is located $1.5\text{ m}$ ahead at zero velocity does not dictate whether the machine should halt, navigate around it, or inspect it. A high-level policy or remote operator evaluates the state belief to issue a structured intent lease. The boundary contract specifies that the goal is valid only within a defined geometric volume and only for a finite duration, such as an analytical lease window of $500\text{ ms}$. The rejection test at this boundary prevents stale objective persistence. If an upstream deliberative model stalls or enters an autoregressive loop, the lease expires on the monotonic clock, and the planner refuses to synthesize motion for a goal whose authorization has elapsed.

The fourth handoff, Plan, converts an authorized intent lease into a time-indexed sequence of candidate waypoints with declared feasibility assumptions and a validity horizon, because a goal does not supply a physically executable trajectory. An intent specifying a target coordinate provides no torque profiles, no kinematic joint paths, and no guarantee that intervening geometry is free of collision. The planning stage samples or optimizes a candidate motion profile over a preview horizon, such as sixteen steps across a $320\text{ ms}$ analytical window, explicitly checking joint limits and continuity. The rejection test at this interface isolates kinodynamic failure from goal selection. If the planner produces a trajectory that demands excessive joint acceleration or crosses an obstacle boundary, the candidate is rejected immediately without relitigating the overarching goal, prompting an immediate replan or an in-place deceleration.

The fifth handoff, Enforce, emits either an allowed, bounded physical command or an explicit refusal with a structured diagnostic reason, because a planned trajectory does not grant execution permission. The trajectory planner operates on mathematical models and discrete time steps, which cannot account for instantaneous current spikes, sudden thermal limits in motor windings, or microsecond obstacle intrusions. The enforcement stage sits on dedicated real-time silicon, evaluating the candidate proposal against hard physical invariants at a high control cadence, such as $1000\text{ Hz}$. Its contract is absolute. The enforcer either passes a minimally modified command that preserves forward invariance, or it refuses the proposal and commands an immediate safe stopping profile. This is the only handoff in the entire machine that connects to inverter power stages and commands physical energy.[^fn_safety_standards_ch03]

Maintaining the integrity of these five handoffs requires carrying age, uncertainty, and validity metadata across every boundary rather than stripping them after initial computation. When a perception module extracts a 3D coordinate and discards the measurement covariance and capture timestamp, downstream planning is forced to treat a stale, uncertain extrapolation as an exact, instantaneous ground truth. In an analytical scenario where an image captured $120\text{ ms}$ ago yields a point estimate without an age tag, a trajectory planner will optimize a high-speed motion based on where the obstacle was, rather than where its growing uncertainty cone dictates it could be. Preserving metadata through the entire chain allows each subsequent stage to evaluate its own rejection criteria against the true degradation of the underlying evidence.

The interface schemas, temporal limits, deterministic rejection tests, and safe fallback behaviors across this chain are formalized in @tbl-03-five-handoffs.

| Handoff Stage | Input Contract (Payload & Provenance) | Output Contract (Artifact & Metadata) | Temporal Deadline & Validity ($\tau_{\text{valid}}$) | Deterministic Checker & Rejection Test | Safe Fallback & Interception Mechanism |
|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|:---|
| **1. Observe** (Transduction) | Raw physical transducer signals (photons, magnetic fields, strain voltages) | Timestamped sensory frame ($I \in \mathbb{R}^{C \times H \times W}$, sensor ID, monotonic clock $t_0$, CRC) | $t_{\text{acq}} \le 16.7\text{ ms}$ (at $60\text{ Hz}$), zero transport delay | Hardware CRC checksum test, frame-drop counter, optical saturation detector | Drop corrupted frame; hold preceding valid observation with `stale_flag=1` |
| **2. Estimate** (Perception / State) | Multi-modal observation stream with hardware timestamps | Metric state belief ($\hat{\mathbf{x}} \in SE(3)$, covariance $\mathbf{P} \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$, age $t_{\text{age}}$) | $t_{\text{exec}} \le 35.0\text{ ms}$, validity $\tau_{\text{valid}} \le 50.0\text{ ms}$ | Freshness check ($t_{\text{age}} \le \tau_{\text{max}}$), covariance trace bound ($\text{Tr}(\mathbf{P}) \le \sigma_{\text{max}}^2$), NaN/Inf scan | Suppress ungrounded belief update; propagate dead-reckoning kinematic prior |
| **3. Intend** (Deliberation / Goal) | Verified state belief $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$, mission directive, operational mode | Structured Intent Lease ($\mathcal{G} \subset SE(3)$, priority $p \in [1,5]$, expiration $t_{\text{expire}}$) | $t_{\text{delib}} \le 200\text{ ms}$, lease lifetime $\tau_{\text{lease}} \le 500\text{ ms}$ | Monotonic expiration check ($t_{\text{sys}} < t_{\text{expire}}$), cryptographic authorization verify, workspace bound | Invalidate expired intent lease; transition to station-keeping idle state |
| **4. Plan** (Trajectory Synthesis) | Active intent lease $\mathcal{G}$, dynamic obstacle map, kinematic state $\hat{\mathbf{x}}$ | Time-indexed candidate trajectory $(\mathbf{q}_{1:H}, \dot{\mathbf{q}}_{1:H}, \ddot{\mathbf{q}}_{1:H}, \tau_{\text{horizon}})$ | $t_{\text{synth}} \le 40.0\text{ ms}$, preview horizon $H \cdot \Delta t \le 320\text{ ms}$ | Kinematic limit verification ($|\dot{\mathbf{q}}| \le \dot{\mathbf{q}}_{\text{max}}$), continuous collision swept-volume test | Reject infeasible candidate chunk; command maximum-rate controlled deceleration |
| **5. Enforce** (Physical Actuation) | Candidate trajectory chunk, joint encoder feedback, proximity monitors ($1000\text{ Hz}$) | Admissible actuator command ($\boldsymbol{\tau}_{\text{cmd}} \in \mathbb{R}^m$, phase currents) or structured refusal code | $t_{\text{ctrl}} \le 1.0\text{ ms}$ ($<10\,\mu\text{s}$ jitter, bare-metal SRAM) | Control Barrier Function QP ($\dot{h} + \gamma h \ge 0$), torque slew rate limiter, motor thermal model | Intercept unsafe proposal; inject closed-form safe braking torques directly to inverters |

: **The Five Handoffs Input/Output Interface Contract Matrix.** Formal specification of data payload schemas, provenance metadata, temporal latency budgets, deterministic rejection tests, and safe fallback behaviors across the sense-estimate-intend-plan-enforce pipeline. {#tbl-03-five-handoffs}

These five stages represent logical system functions rather than separate physical processors, software threads, or distinct machine learning models. A designer might map each function to an independent hardware subsystem, or collapse several functions into a single deep neural network, such as an end-to-end vision-language-action policy that takes camera pixels and directly outputs candidate joint trajectories. What that architectural collapse costs is not inference speed, but the intermediate inspection points, explicit expirations, and localized rejection tests that the partitioned contracts guarantee. When an end-to-end policy directly links perception to trajectory generation, the machine loses the ability to reject a stale observation before intent formation, or to audit whether an erratic command stemmed from perceptual hallucination or kinematic infeasibility. As contrasted in @fig-03-five-handoffs, collapsing functions into a learned black box does not eliminate the physical dependencies; it merely conceals them behind an interface that can no longer refuse invalid inputs before they reach the motor drives.

In modern physical AI hardware platforms—such as the **Physical AI Kit (Arduino UNO Q reference realization)**—these five functional stages map directly across the heterogeneous dual-brain silicon boundary. Handoffs 1 through 4 ($\text{Observe} \to \text{Estimate} \to \text{Intend} \to \text{Plan}$) execute within the unprivileged software environment of the Linux MPU (ARM Cortex-A). The MPU processes high-bandwidth camera streams, computes 3D state beliefs $\hat{\mathbf{x}} \in SE(3)$, converts task directives into expiring intent leases ($\mathcal{L}_{\text{intent}}$), and synthesizes candidate trajectory chunks ($\mathbf{A}_{t:t+H}$) using learned diffusion models or spline generators. The non-negotiable **Proposal–Permission Privilege Boundary** sits precisely between Handoff 4 (Plan) and Handoff 5 (Enforce). Candidate trajectory plans cross the boundary over shared-SRAM mailboxes via the Remote Processor Messaging (RPMSG) protocol, carrying monotonic sequence IDs, capture timestamps, lease expirations ($\tau_{\text{lease}}$), and CRC32 checksums. Handoff 5 (Enforce) resides exclusively on the isolated bare-metal MCU (STM32 ARM Cortex-M), where an active-set Control Barrier Function QP solver evaluates safety invariants and dynamic stopping clearances ($d_{\text{stop}} \le D_{\text{clear}}$) at $1000\text{ Hz}$ with sub-microsecond jitter. Only the MCU possesses physical wiring and register write authority over the pulse-width modulation (PWM) timers that energize motor inverters. If the MPU suffers memory bus stalls, driver lockups, or lease expiration, the MCU refuses the unverified proposal ($\bot$) and executes a deterministic safe stop.

![**The Canonical Five Handoffs Architecture and Boundary Rejection Gates vs. Collapsed End-to-End Latent Pipeline.** (Panel A) The canonical modular chain enforces five distinct functional contracts: Observe (timestamped raw evidence $O_t$), Estimate (metric state belief $\hat{x}_t \in SE(3)$ and covariance $\Sigma_t$), Intend (semantic goal lease $\mathcal{L}_{\text{intent}}$ with expiration $t_{\text{expire}}$), Plan (candidate action chunk $\mathbf{A}_{t:t+H}$ with $C^2$ spline bounds), and Enforce (active-set barrier QP solver). Each interface features a dedicated rejection gate (RG-1 through RG-5) that intercepts dropped packets, tracking divergence, expired leases, kinematic infeasibilities, or barrier violations before unprivileged proposals (dashed paths) can reach physical actuators. (Panel B) A collapsed end-to-end policy maps raw pixels directly to uninspected motor torques, forfeiting four critical intermediate inspection points and transferring the entire burden of sensory validation, state estimation, and lease verification onto low-level reflex filters.](figures/fig03_five_handoffs.svg){#fig-03-five-handoffs fig-pos="t" width=90%}

The entire architecture reduces to a single operational principle. A prediction is not a decision, a decision is not a command, and a command is not yet an action. Perception and memory produce predictions about what the environment was and how it might evolve. Semantic reasoning turns those predictions into a bounded decision about what objective to pursue. Trajectory planning translates that decision into a candidate command. Only real-time enforcement possesses the authority to turn a candidate command into a physical action that expends electrical power, applies mechanical force, and irreversibly changes the state of the physical world. Understanding each handoff as an enforceable contract provides the foundation for determining whether a learned component, regardless of its benchmark accuracy or inference speed, can survive the physical demands and failure modes of an embodied machine.
<!-- END -->

## Systems Stress-Tests {#sec-brain-3-9}

<!-- SECTION 3.9 -->
<!-- claim: A part can be accurate, fast, and still unusable. -->
<!-- covers: In an analytical transport case, compare a $40\text{ ms}$ mean with a $180\text{ ms}$ tail at $1.5\text{ m/s}$ and compute the additional $0.21\text{ m}$ traveled before a proposal arrives. -->
<!-- covers: Given one hundred outputs reported near $0.90$ confidence with sixty-four observed successes, compute the $0.26$ calibration gap and decide whether any useful abstention threshold remains. -->
<!-- covers: Compare two models with equal task success but different peak memory and tail latency, then select the one that preserves the larger @sec-body margins. -->
<!-- covers: Reevaluate a model that meets its deadline in isolation after camera traffic and retained context contend for the same memory bandwidth. -->
<!-- covers: Decide the disposition of a semantically plausible plan whose intent lease has expired before enforcement receives it. -->

<!-- BEGIN -->
A learned component can achieve high benchmark accuracy, report millisecond-scale average execution times, and remain unusable inside a physical machine. When a model operates in a closed loop with sensors and actuators, its engineering value is bounded by its tail latency, its calibration under distribution shift, its memory footprint under bus contention, and its adherence to temporal contracts. Evaluating a learned model for embodied deployment requires testing it not as an isolated statistical estimator, but as an integrated component that competes for shared silicon and commands physical mass. The following five analytical stress-tests examine whether a candidate model can survive the physical and operational demands of embodied execution:

- *Stress-Test 1: The Tail Latency Gap in Motion (Computational Delay as Physical Displacement).* In an analytical transport case, an autonomous wheeled cargo platform operates in an industrial logistics corridor at a steady forward velocity $v_0 = 1.5\text{ m/s}$. The platform senses obstacles using an onboard stereo camera pair and generates candidate collision-avoidance paths through a learned local trajectory model. When profiled in isolation on an idle processor, the model reports an average inference latency of $\bar{t} = 40.0\text{ ms}$. Under live operating conditions with concurrent operating system tasks, measured tail latency reaches $P_{99} = 180.0\text{ ms}$.
  - *The Diagnostic Test:* Sizing safety buffers against mean latency converts computational jitter directly into uncommanded physical displacement ($\Delta d = v_0 \Delta t$). During a $P_{99}$ tail event, the vehicle coasts unguided for an additional distance $\Delta d_{\text{react}} = 1.5\text{ m/s} \times (0.180\text{ s} - 0.040\text{ s}) = 0.21\text{ m}$ before a new avoidance proposal reaches the safety enforcer. This $21.0\text{ cm}$ displacement directly compresses the remaining braking clearance, turning a certified stopping trajectory into an unavoidable barrier collision.
  - *The Systems Verdict:* Tail Latency Invariant. Moving mass cannot pause while an accelerator clears an arbitration stall. In a closed physical loop, tail latency ($P_{99}$) rather than average throughput ($\bar{t}$) is the binding constraint that governs physical clearance buffers and maximum operational velocity.
- *Stress-Test 2: Uncalibrated Confidence in Contact Tasks (The Softmax Illusion).* An articulated six-axis robotic manipulator performs precision bin-picking and placement of machined metal castings. The learned grasping policy outputs candidate end-effector poses accompanied by a predicted success probability $\hat{p} \in [0, 1]$. In an analytical evaluation across 100 grasp attempts where the model reports confidence in the narrow range of $\hat{p} \approx 0.90$, physical execution on the fixture yields 64 successful seating operations and 36 dropped or misaligned parts.
  - *The Diagnostic Test:* The system supervisor uses predicted confidence to trigger an abstention policy, delegating low-confidence grasps to an operator or an exploratory tactile scan. The $0.26$ calibration gap between reported confidence ($0.90$) and empirical success ($0.64$) destroys the monotonic probability ranking required for selective execution, passing hazardous proposals downstream to mechanical actuators while providing an illusion of safety.
  - *The Systems Verdict:* Calibration Gating Law. Raw softmax outputs and logit scores represent ungrounded network activation states rather than true physical probabilities. A learned model cannot hold selective authority over mechanical actuators without empirical calibration curves (such as isotonic regression or Platt scaling) validated across the target operational domain.
- *Stress-Test 3: Hardware Margin Preservation under Equal Task Success (Physical Resource Footprint).* An embedded controller regulates an exothermic chemical process by modulating a high-pressure proportional mixing valve. Two candidate learned policies achieve an identical $94\%$ task success rate in closed-loop process simulation. Model A (a transformer-based policy) requires $3.2\text{ GB}$ of peak DRAM, consumes $14.0\text{ W}$ of compute power, and exhibits a tail latency of $P_{99} = 85.0\text{ ms}$. Model B (a compact recurrent convolutional policy) requires $680\text{ MB}$ of peak DRAM, consumes $4.5\text{ W}$, and exhibits a tail latency of $P_{99} = 28.0\text{ ms}$. The embedded system provides $4.0\text{ GB}$ of total unified memory, a $15.0\text{ W}$ thermal dissipation ceiling, and a valve update deadline of $50.0\text{ ms}$.
  - *The Diagnostic Test:* Although standard benchmark rankings treat the two models as equivalent, Model A consumes $80\%$ of system memory (leaving only $800\text{ MB}$ for I/O buffers), pushes thermal dissipation within $1.0\text{ W}$ of the throttling limit, and overruns the $50.0\text{ ms}$ real-time actuation deadline by $35.0\text{ ms}$. Model B preserves $3.32\text{ GB}$ of DRAM headroom, leaves $10.5\text{ W}$ of thermal reserve, and meets the deadline with a $22.0\text{ ms}$ safety margin.
  - *The Systems Verdict:* Physical Resource Margin Invariant. Task accuracy is merely an admission threshold, not a selection criterion. When functional capability is equal, physical systems engineering selects the model architecture that maximizes physical margins across memory headroom, thermal dissipation, and timing buffers.
- *Stress-Test 4: Memory Contention under Concurrent Sensor Ingest (The LPDDR5 Bandwidth Wall).* An autonomous inspection rover carries four high-resolution global-shutter cameras streaming raw, uncompressed video frames via Direct Memory Access (DMA) into unified system memory at $30\text{ Hz}$, generating $1.99\text{ GB/s}$ of continuous ingest traffic. An onboard vision-language policy for surface flaw detection meets its $45.0\text{ ms}$ inference deadline when profiled in isolation with static input tensors already resident in memory.
  - *The Diagnostic Test:* During live operation, continuous sensor DMA transfers and the retrieval of retained historical context tokens compete for access to the shared LPDDR5 memory bus ($25.6\text{ GB/s}$ sustained limit). Memory arbitration latency inflates tensor read cycles, stretching neural inference time from $45.0\text{ ms}$ to $78.0\text{ ms}$ and overrunning the $60.0\text{ ms}$ planning deadline.
  - *The Systems Verdict:* Shared Memory Bandwidth Invariant. An inference accelerator does not own the memory bus. A learned component evaluated in isolation provides an invalid timing contract once embedded in an integrated machine with active sensor DMA streams and concurrent memory traffic.
- *Stress-Test 5: Disposition of an Expired Intent Lease (Temporal Validity and Enforcement Authority).* A dual-arm industrial robot in an automated assembly cell receives a high-level intent lease to seat a structural bracket onto a moving conveyor fixture. The semantic reasoning stage issues the lease with an explicit timestamp and a validity window of $\tau_{\text{lease}} = 200.0\text{ ms}$. Because of operating system thread preemption and trajectory interpolation overhead, the resulting candidate joint trajectory packet arrives at the real-time enforcement controller $245.0\text{ ms}$ after lease generation ($45.0\text{ ms}$ past expiration). Geometric verification confirms the proposed path is smooth, kinematically valid, and collision-free against the static workcell model.
  - *The Diagnostic Test:* Although the trajectory appears geometrically optimal and semantically sound, the authorization lease has expired. Conveyor movement and dynamic environment changes during unmonitored delays invalidate the assumptions under which the plan was generated. Allowing the enforcement layer to waive lease expiration based on perceived trajectory quality destroys the architectural boundary between unverified deliberation and physical action.
  - *The Systems Verdict:* Temporal Validity Invariant. The real-time safety enforcer evaluates authority and temporal validity, never semantic plausibility. An expired proposal is an invalid proposal; the nervous system must reject late packets deterministically and fall back to a safe holding reflex.
<!-- END -->

## Summary {#sec-brain-3-10}

<!-- SECTION 3.10 -->
<!-- claim: Part II pins down what each handoff must be right about. -->
<!-- covers: Restate the learned component as an interface contract plus a measured resource and degradation envelope. -->
<!-- covers: State that learning is admitted only when its measured capability gain justifies the uncertainty and system cost it introduces. -->
<!-- covers: Preserve the distinction among scores, probabilities, samples, and calibrated uncertainty. -->
<!-- covers: Carry forward the separation between deterministically detectable contract violations and semantic failures that lack timely runtime labels. -->
<!-- covers: Restate the five handoffs through the artifact each produces and the check made possible at its boundary. -->
<!-- covers: Hand @sec-nervous the unresolved questions of invocation rate, tracking rate, enforcement rate, and which path may command physical energy. -->

<!-- BEGIN -->
A learned model enters a physical architecture as a bounded software component rather than an autonomous decision maker. An engineer specifies the model by its interface contract, its resource footprint, and its degradation envelope under stress. The interface contract establishes input tensor dimensions, sensor coordinate conventions, output ranges, and deterministic execution deadlines, such as an inference budget of $40\text{ ms}$ at $P_{99}$ latency on a dedicated accelerator. The resource envelope accounts for memory footprint, dynamic random-access memory bandwidth consumed during concurrent direct memory access transfers, and thermal dissipation under continuous inference load. Under autoregressive token generation, the operational arithmetic intensity collapses to $1\text{--}4\text{ FLOPs/byte}$, making deep foundation models (7B--55B parameters) strictly memory-bandwidth bound and confining them behind the $204.8\text{ GB/s}$ LPDDR5 memory wall to $1\text{--}5\text{ Hz}$ execution cadences on edge silicon. Specifying the model as a physical component strips away assumptions of generalized reasoning and leaves a concrete engineering artifact whose memory traffic, execution timing, and error margins can be budgeted against physical limits.

System design admits a learned model only when the measured capability gain over deterministic alternatives justifies the uncertainty and system cost the network introduces. Where classical kinematics, convex optimization, or deterministic state machines solve an engineering problem within resource budgets, a physical system relies on them. Machine learning is reserved for functions where explicit physical and geometric modeling becomes intractable, including parsing unstructured visual scenes, mapping semantic instructions to spatial references, and synthesizing multi-contact manipulation plans across unmodeled friction regimes. Admitting this capability introduces non-zero tail error rates, statistical opacity, and non-deterministic failure modes. Every watt drawn by an accelerator, every millisecond consumed by a forward pass, and every watchdog monitor required to inspect intermediate outputs represents an ongoing architectural cost that must be purchased with a demonstrable capability gain.

Integrating learned outputs into physical execution requires strict discipline regarding what those outputs represent mathematically. Raw logit values and softmax vectors represent uncalibrated scores rather than true likelihoods of physical reality. A model output assigning a confidence score of $0.98$ to an obstacle class indicates only the internal activation state of the neural network, not a $98\text{ percent}$ probability of physical occupancy in the workspace. Generative policies produce individual sample trajectories drawn from an implicit distribution, offering no structural guarantee of temporal consistency, smoothness, or dynamic feasibility between consecutive execution cycles. Calibrated uncertainty requires explicit statistical guarantees established over a target operational domain, mapping predicted confidence intervals to empirical error frequencies under realistic sensor noise. Treating uncalibrated scores or stochastic samples as calibrated probabilities allows unverified statistical artifacts to enter safety-critical physical pipelines.

A physical architecture must separate contract violations that can be detected deterministically at runtime from semantic failures that carry no timely runtime labels. Deterministic contract violations reveal themselves immediately through synchronous checks. An intent lease arriving $45\text{ ms}$ past its $200\text{ ms}$ expiration window, an inference thread exceeding its $60\text{ ms}$ compute deadline, an arithmetic overflow producing floating-point invalid values, or a joint velocity command exceeding physical actuator limits can all be caught and halted by deterministic logic in the nervous system. Semantic failures, by contrast, generate syntactically valid outputs that are physically or contextually incorrect. A vision network that misclassifies a glass barrier as open traversable space or a trajectory generator that outputs a smooth, kinematically valid path toward the wrong target produces tensors that satisfy all schema, range, and latency checks. Because semantic truth cannot be verified through runtime telemetry alone, the architecture cannot rely on the learned model to evaluate its own mistakes. The machine must guard against semantic errors through downstream physical envelopes, geometric workspace boundaries, and hard mechanical interlocks.

Across the machine, five distinct handoffs structure the flow of authority from raw sensory inputs to physical work, each defined by the artifact it produces and the deterministic verification made possible at its boundary. The first handoff converts raw sensor bitstreams into a synchronized spatial-temporal state estimate, producing a structured representation whose timestamp monotonicity, sensor freshness, and frame calibration can be audited prior to fusion. The second handoff maps the estimated state into a discrete task goal, emitting an intent lease whose cryptographic validity, authorization scope, and temporal lifetime are verified against system policy. The third handoff translates the intent lease into a nominal candidate trajectory, generating a sequence of spatial waypoints whose kinematic feasibility and static collision clearances are checked through geometric calculation. The fourth handoff passes candidate paths through dynamic safety filters, yielding an admissible reference command whose stability certificates, acceleration limits, and control barrier functions are validated before actuation. The fifth handoff delivers the reference command to low-level feedback controllers, producing pulse-width modulation signals and motor phase currents whose tracking errors, winding temperatures, and torque limits are enforced at kilohertz rates.

In physical realizations such as the **Physical AI Kit (Arduino UNO Q)**, this five-handoff pipeline maps onto a dual-brain hardware partitioning: the unprivileged Linux MPU hosts the memory-bound perception, intent, and trajectory planners, transmitting candidate proposals ($p_t$) across an isolated RPMSG mailbox to the bare-metal MCU. The MCU evaluates Control Barrier Functions and dynamic stopping distances at $1000\text{ Hz}$, retaining exclusive electrical authority over motor inverter gate drives. These handoffs define what data structures traverse system boundaries, but they leave the operational timing and authority of the machine unresolved. A learned planning model evaluated at an invocation rate of $10\text{ Hz}$ cannot directly command an actuator whose electric current loop must run at $20\text{ kHz}$ to prevent acoustic noise and thermal breakdown. An emergency stop circuit operating on a $2\text{ ms}$ hardware loop enforces safety on a different temporal scale than an optimization layer checking control barrier functions at $100\text{ Hz}$. @sec-nervous examines how the nervous system arbitrates these disparate timescales. It details how the nervous system separates the slow advisory path of the learned brain from the fast deterministic loop of the body, establishing which timing loop maintains tracking, which layer enforces safety constraints, and which physical circuit retains final authority over actuator energy. Once that physical nervous system is constructed, Part II pins down what each handoff must be right about, examining the data distributions, training objectives, and verification criteria required to make learned models dependable components in a physical world.
<!-- END -->

[^fn_symbolic_connectionist]: Historical Context: The architectural tension between explicit symbolic logic and learned distributed representations traces back to the inception of cybernetics. In 1943, Warren McCulloch and Walter Pitts demonstrated that idealized networks of binary threshold neurons could compute arbitrary logical propositions, laying the theoretical foundation for symbolic automata [@mcculloch1943logical]. By 1958, Frank Rosenblatt's Perceptron introduced statistical weight adjustment from continuous sensory data [@rosenblatt1958perceptron]. The modern Physical AI paradigm resolves this classic schism by partitioning responsibilities: high-capacity connectionist networks serve as heuristic proposal engines, while symbolic, formal-methods-based supervisors enforce deterministic safety invariants.

[^fn_lipschitz_calibration]: Mathematical Subtlety: A deep neural network $f_\theta: \mathcal{X} \to \mathcal{Y}$ parameterized by weights $\theta$ is generally non-Lipschitz or exhibits an impractically large Lipschitz constant $L$ satisfying $\|f_\theta(x_1) - f_\theta(x_2)\| \le L \|x_1 - x_2\|$, making output sensitivity highly non-uniform across the input manifold. Furthermore, calibration metrics such as Expected Calibration Error ($\text{ECE}$) evaluate marginal expectations over a static validation distribution $P(X, Y)$; they provide no pointwise guarantee that $\mathbb{P}(Y = \hat{Y} \mid X = x^*) \ge 1 - \epsilon$ for a specific operational query $x^*$, particularly under localized sensor anomalies or adversarial perturbations.

[^fn_npu_memory_wall]: Hardware Nuance: In edge System-on-Chip (SoC) platforms (such as the NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin or modern automotive domain controllers), the CPU, GPU, and deep learning accelerator (NPU) share a unified memory controller and LPDDR5 physical interface. While tensor systolic arrays achieve peak Tera-Operations Per Second ($\text{TOPS}$) on compute-bound matrix multiplications whose tiles fit in on-chip SRAM, memory-bound layers (such as depthwise convolutions or un-fused multi-head attention projections) are throttled by external DRAM bandwidth. High-priority asynchronous DMA bursts from multi-camera MIPI interfaces can stall tensor fetch pipelines at the memory crossbar, inflating $P_{99}$ execution tails well beyond isolated benchmark figures.

[^fn_safety_standards_ch03]: Statutory Standard: Established functional safety standards strictly mandate deterministic containment for non-verifiable software components. Under ISO 26262 (Road Vehicles -- Functional Safety), deep neural networks cannot achieve high Automotive Safety Integrity Levels (such as ASIL-D) in isolation due to their inability to provide formal structural coverage (such as MC/DC). Consequently, standards such as UL 4600 (Standard for Safety for the Evaluation of Autonomous Products) and ISO 21448 (Safety of the Intended Functionality, SOTIF) require an independent, deterministic supervisory channel—architecturally decoupled from the learned model—to detect hazardous proposals and enforce a minimum risk condition before physical execution.
